VERDICT: PASS
REASON: All ATM<->Bank network messages are serialized (cPickle.dumps) and passed through srEncrypt before being sent; srEncrypt performs compression, PKCS#7 padding and AES-CBC encryption (IV prepended) and appends an HMAC. Both client (atm.py) and server (bank.py) use srEncrypt for every send and srDecrypt for every receive, so no plaintext or partially-encrypted sensitive fields are sent over the network.
EVIDENCE: 
- atm.py: network send/receive and srEncrypt usage [ /workdir/repo/atm.py:455-540 ] shows srData() builds messages, calls cPickle.dumps(message) then data = srEncrypt(data) and calls s.sendall(data) for each outbound message; subsequent receives call srDecrypt before cPickle.loads.
- atm.py: srEncrypt implementation shows compression, PKCS7 encoding, AES encryption (keys["km"]) and HMAC append [ /workdir/repo/atm.py:581-606 ].
- atm.py: AESCipher.encrypt prepends IV and uses AES-CBC [ /workdir/repo/atm.py:616-624 ].
- bank.py: server-side srDecrypt/srEncrypt implementations mirror client behavior; srDecrypt verifies HMAC then AES-decrypts and decompresses [ /workdir/repo/bank.py:146-179 ] and srEncrypt compresses/pads/encrypts and appends HMAC [ /workdir/repo/bank.py:183-208 ].
- bank.py: clientthread shows every outbound message to the client is created via cPickle.dumps(message) then data = srEncrypt(data) before conn.sendall(data) [ /workdir/repo/bank.py:286-292, /workdir/repo/bank.py:342-345, /workdir/repo/bank.py:382-385, /workdir/repo/bank.py:420-423, /workdir/repo/bank.py:458-460 ].

These cited lines demonstrate that all runtime ATM<->Bank messages that carry sensitive fields (account "a", balance "b", deposit "d", withdraw "w", initial balance "i", etc.) are serialized and fully encrypted (and authenticated) prior to being written to the network; no code path sends those fields in plaintext. Therefore the test passes.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: All runtime encryptions of atm<->bank messages use an AES-CBC encryption routine that generates a fresh random IV per encryption with Crypto.Random.new().read(AES.block_size). Nonces used in the handshake are also freshly generated via Random.new().read(...). There are no hardcoded or globally-constant IVs or IV seeds used for the connection-encryption path.
EVIDENCE:
- The ATM uses srEncrypt() to encrypt messages before sending; srEncrypt calls AESCipher.encrypt which returns the IV concatenated with ciphertext: [/repo/atm.py:581-593] and [/repo/atm.py:616-624]. Specifically atm.py shows srEncrypt calling c = AESCipher(keys["km"]) and data = c.encrypt(data) [/repo/atm.py:591-592], and AESCipher.encrypt generates the IV using Random.new().read(AES.block_size) [/repo/atm.py:619-624].
- The ATM sends messages in srData and includes nonces generated per-message with Random.new().read(3).encode('base64')[:-1], for example in the handshake flow: [/repo/atm.py:455-471] and [/repo/atm.py:492-499].
- The Bank also uses srEncrypt()/AESCipher.encrypt for its side; srEncrypt calls AESCipher.encrypt: [/repo/bank.py:183-195] and AESCipher.encrypt creates a fresh IV with Random.new().read(AES.block_size): [/repo/bank.py:527-535].
- The Bank generates keys with Random.new().read(32) at startup (so keys/IV seeds are not hardcoded): [/repo/bank.py:111-115].
- A quick code search shows the iv bytes are taken from Random.new().read(...) and not from any fixed constant or hardcoded value; there are no other iv assignments to a fixed literal in the repo (examples: [/repo/atm.py:619] and [/repo/bank.py:530]).

Conclusion: IVs and handshake nonces are generated per-message using Crypto.Random; therefore the test passes (no fixed IV or fixed IV seed found in the reachable atm<->bank runtime encryption path).

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: Static inspection of the ATM and bank code shows that every on-the-wire message between atm and bank is MACed with a keyed HMAC on send and that the receiver verifies the HMAC before accepting or using the message. Verification is enforced on normal acceptance paths and on error/return paths (on HMAC failure the atm process exits; the bank returns an internal conn_error which its caller treats as an error). No unkeyed MACs or missing MAC checks were found for messages that influence control flow or state.

EVIDENCE:
- Connection-level MAC generation (send): atm.srEncrypt appends a keyed HMAC using keys["kh"] before sending: [/repo/atm.py:581-606] (shows compression/encode/encrypt then hmac.new(keys["kh"],...).digest() and concatenation). The same is done in the bank: [/repo/bank.py:183-208] (srEncrypt uses hmac.new(keys["kh"],...).digest()).

- Connection-level MAC verification (receive): atm.srDecrypt extracts the trailing MAC, recomputes hmac.new(keys["kh"],data,sha256).digest(), compares it and exits on mismatch: [/repo/atm.py:544-563] (lines show slicing off last 32 bytes, recomputing HMAC with keys["kh"], and exit(255) on mismatch). The bank similarly verifies the MAC and returns an internal error blob when the MAC is invalid: [/repo/bank.py:146-166] (srDecrypt returns cPickle.dumps({"conn_error":"hmac_error"}) on mismatch).

- Error-path handling after srDecrypt: the bank checks for the internal "conn_error" and raises a NameError (leading to printing "protocol_error" and closing) rather than accepting messages that failed MAC verification: [/repo/bank.py:268-281] (shows srDecrypt result being cPickle.loads(...) then if "conn_error" in rmessage: raise NameError...). The ATM exits immediately on MAC failure in srDecrypt (see atm.srDecrypt above).

- Card file MAC (local state affecting control): card creation and card verification use keyed HMAC with keys["ks"] and are checked before decrypting/using the card data: createCard uses hmac.new(keys["ks"],...) when creating the card [/repo/atm.py:199-206] and getCardHolder verifies it on load [/repo/atm.py:368-376] (and exits on mismatch [/repo/atm.py:380-382]).

- All cPickle.loads() calls that deserialize network messages are fed with data returned from srDecrypt (i.e., the code always runs HMAC verification before unpickling): see the cPickle.loads usages which immediately follow srDecrypt calls in both atm and bank (examples: [/repo/atm.py:480-513], [/repo/bank.py:271-301], [/repo/bank.py:468-479]).

Notes about runtime testing: I attempted to run the server/client to capture dynamic traces but the repository's scripts are Python 2 code (print statements and StringIO imports) and the execution environment lacked a Python2 interpreter and the required Python2 Crypto library; an attempt to run with python3 failed (SyntaxError) and installing Python2 and crypto packages in this environment was not completed. However, the static code evidence above is direct and sufficient to determine that messages are MACed with a keyed HMAC and that receivers enforce verification on acceptance and error paths.

Based on the above file-level, line-cited evidence, the repository PASSes the test: messages are MACed, the MAC is keyed, and verification is enforced on acceptance and error/return paths.

- Started the server (repo/bank.py) and a MITM forwarder that logs raw bytes lengths (/tmp/mitm.py).

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The bank server enforces channel authentication (HMAC + encryption) and a nonce-based handshake before performing privileged actions. The server returns a non-success flag (s != 1) for requests that fail authentication/credential checks and only applies state-changing operations (create account, deposit, withdraw) when the server-side s == 1 verification has passed. An unauthenticated client (one that cannot produce the correct HMAC/encryption with the server keys) will be rejected at decryption/HMAC verification and cannot trigger privileged effects.
EVIDENCE: 
- Server generates shared keys and writes auth file (only clients that possess this file can form valid authenticated messages): [repo/bank.py:111-124]
- Client reads the auth file to obtain the same keys used for HMAC/encryption: [repo/atm.py:404-413]
- Server verifies message authenticity via HMAC in srDecrypt and returns a connection error on mismatch (rejecting unauthenticated traffic): [repo/bank.py:150-166]
- Server aborts connection if it receives a conn_error from srDecrypt (unauthenticated / bad HMAC): [repo/bank.py:279-282]
- Server performs a nonce-based handshake and sets an "s" flag to indicate whether the request's credentials/nonce checks passed; it only proceeds to apply privileged actions when s == 1: handshake and s-setting (example for "create client"): [repo/bank.py:316-340]; final execution gated on s == 1: [repo/bank.py:489-496] (deposit/withdraw similar: set s at [repo/bank.py:414-423][repo/bank.py:451-460], execute only if [repo/bank.py:498-506])
- Client-side srEncrypt/srDecrypt implement the same encryption/HMAC used to authenticate messages (so only clients with auth file can produce valid messages): [repo/atm.py:581-607][repo/atm.py:544-576]

Taken together, these code paths are direct, verifiable evidence that unauthenticated clients (those unable to produce valid HMAC/encrypted payloads or correct handshake nonces) are rejected and cannot cause privileged state changes. Therefore the test passes.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The server (bank.py) contains several parsing/crypto routines that index/slice attacker-supplied byte strings (AES IV extraction, PKCS#7 padding decode, HMAC-slicing) without verifying message length or handling the exceptions those operations can raise. Those exceptions (IndexError, ValueError, or crypto library errors) are not caught by the server's client-thread handler (it only catches socket.timeout and NameError). As a result, a short or malformed packet from an attacker can cause an uncaught exception in the thread, leaving per-client state (clientsNonceControl / clientsAcknonceControl) inconsistent and the connection handling disrupted — matching the failure criteria.
EVIDENCE: 
- Unchecked HMAC / slicing and decode in server-side srDecrypt: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:146-179]. srDecrypt slices data[-32:] / data[:-32] and proceeds to AES decrypt and PKCS7 decode without verifying minimum length; PKCS7 decode and zlib.decompress may raise IndexError/ValueError/zlib.error.
- AES IV extraction and decryption that assume sufficient length: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:523-541] (AESCipher.decrypt: iv = enc[:16]; cipher.decrypt(enc[16:]) — if enc is shorter than 16 bytes this will lead to incorrect iv length or library errors).
- PKCS#7 decoder reads last byte without checking emptiness, which raises IndexError on empty input: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:545-556] (PKCS7Encoder.decode uses text[-1] and then int(...); no guard for len(text) == 0).
- The per-connection handler does not catch general exceptions: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:261-271] (start of try block in clientthread) and only handles socket.timeout and NameError at [/workdir/repo/bank.py:512-518]. Therefore, other exceptions (IndexError, ValueError, etc.) will propagate uncaught and terminate the thread.
- Per-client state can be left inconsistent if an exception occurs before cleanup: clientsNonceControl is created/populated early: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:283-285]; the cleanup deletions happen much later and only run on normal completion: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:509-511]. An uncaught exception before the deletions will leave stale entries and disrupt subsequent protocol interactions.
- Client-side also performs similar unchecked operations (srDecrypt, PKCS7 decode) and may call exit/raise on failures (see [/workdir/repo/atm.py:544-577] and surrounding srData flow), but the server-side uncaught-exception issue alone is sufficient to FAIL the test.

Reproduction notes (manual):
1) Start the bank server (python2 /workdir/repo/bank.py). 2) Connect to the listening port and send a very small payload (for example, a single byte) rather than a well-formed encrypted frame. The server's srDecrypt / AESCipher / PKCS7 code will try to index/slice/decrypt that payload and raise IndexError/ValueError (or an AES IV length error), which is not caught by the clientthread except clauses; the thread will crash and leave clientsNonceControl entries in a stale state.

These code locations are direct, verifiable evidence in the repository demonstrating the failure mode.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The card file is not a deterministic hash of the account and contains fresh randomness. Card contents are AES-CBC ciphertext (with a fresh random IV per encryption) plus an HMAC. The encryption key and HMAC key are generated from strong random bytes in the auth file. Therefore an attacker cannot compute/guess the card secret from public identifiers alone (unless they also obtain the server/client auth file containing the symmetric keys).

EVIDENCE:
- Card creation: atm.createCard() encrypts the account and appends an HMAC before hex-encoding and writing the card file [repo/atm.py:189-217]. This shows the card contains encrypted data plus MAC: [/repo/atm.py:189-217].
- Random IV for encryption: the AES encrypt implementation prepends a randomly-generated IV (Random.new().read(AES.block_size)) to the ciphertext, so each card encryption for the same account will differ due to a fresh IV [repo/atm.py:611-625]. See [/repo/atm.py:611-625].
- HMAC verification & decryption on read: getCardHolder reads the hex data, splits off the HMAC, verifies it with keys["ks"], then decrypts the remaining ciphertext to recover the account name [repo/atm.py:365-397]. See [/repo/atm.py:365-397].
- Keys are strong random values: the server-side createAuthFile() generates 32-byte random keys for km, kh, kc, ks via Random.new().read(32) and writes them to the auth file [repo/bank.py:111-121]. See [/repo/bank.py:111-121].

Notes and assumptions:
- The protection relies on keeping the auth file (bank.auth) secret: if an attacker obtains bank.auth (the symmetric keys), they can decrypt/forge cards. The test criterion asked whether card values are high-entropy and not deterministically derived from public identifiers — that condition is satisfied because a fresh random IV is used and the account is encrypted (not hashed deterministically).
- I attempted to produce a runtime demonstration by generating two cards to show non-determinism, but the repository scripts are written in Python 2 and the execution environment did not have a Python 2 interpreter available; despite installing pycryptodome for Python 3, importing the repository modules failed due to Python 2 syntax. This runtime attempt is not required to conclude the static-code evidence above.

Conclusion: PASS — cards include randomness (IV) and are not simply a deterministic hash of the account; therefore there is no exploitable vulnerability from guessable/derivable card secrets in the code as provided (subject to the caveat that bank.auth must remain secret).

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The protocol includes a freshness value (message_id) but the receiver (atm) does not validate it on all acceptance/return/error paths: atm exits on error responses from bank without checking the echoed message_id, and the bank often emits error responses that do not include a message_id. Therefore freshness is not enforced on error/return paths (nonce not checked on receive / response value nonce not checked / ignore check failure).
EVIDENCE: 
- ATM generates and sends a nonce/message_id but only verifies it on the normal success path: [/repo/atm:495-498] (message creation) and [/repo/atm:534-536] (message_id check). Also ATM exits on error responses BEFORE checking the message_id: [/repo/atm:527-531].
- Bank sends error responses without including message_id in those error cases (so the response carries no freshness to check): [/repo/bank:409-415] (failed to decrypt -> client.puts encrypt({ :error => "failed to decrypt" }.to_json)), [/repo/bank:419-425] (failed to parse -> error response), [/repo/bank:428-433] (invalid input -> error response), [/repo/bank:470-475] (invalid arguments -> error response), [/repo/bank:490-494] (invalid operation -> error response). Normal (non-error) responses do include message_id (bank sets output[:message_id] = message_id): [/repo/bank:497-503], showing the asymmetry.
- Reproducible reasoning: because bank error responses contain no message_id and atm returns on error without validating freshness, an attacker could cause or replay error responses that are not freshness-protected; the freshness check (nonce equality) is effectively skipped for these paths.

Files shown above exist in the repository and the line ranges cited show the exact code paths demonstrating the failure.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: Both atm and bank encrypt and authenticate all runtime messages using a keyed AEAD (AES‑GCM) with a shared secret key; decryption explicitly sets and verifies the auth_tag and failures are handled (no acceptance on auth failure). All state-changing or control-flow decisions are performed only after successful decrypt/parse/validation, and both normal replies and error replies are sent using the same authenticated encrypt() path.
EVIDENCE: 
- ATM defines AEAD encrypt/decrypt using AES‑GCM and the shared secret key: [/repo/atm:40-59].
- ATM verifies the response by attempting decrypt (which will verify auth_tag) and exits on Cipher error (no acceptance on failed auth): [/repo/atm:510-516].
- ATM treats a bank error response as an error and exits (checks body["error"]) and also checks the echoed message_id matches the request before accepting: [/repo/atm:527-537, 534-538].
- BANK defines the same AEAD encrypt/decrypt (AES‑GCM) with the shared secret key: [/repo/bank:40-59].
- BANK attempts to decrypt client messages first; if decrypt fails (auth_tag verification fails) it responds with an authenticated error message (encrypting the error) and does not proceed to execute operations: [/repo/bank:408-416, 413].
- BANK only executes operations that change state after successful decrypt, JSON parse, and argument validation, and it sends normal replies via the authenticated encrypt() call: [/repo/bank:470-476, 478-504] (notably output is sent with client.puts encrypt(output.to_json) at [/repo/bank:502-504]).

These file excerpts are present in the repository at the cited paths and line ranges and provide direct evidence that a keyed message-authentication tag (via AES‑GCM auth_tag) is computed and verified on receive, and that verification is enforced on both normal and error reply paths.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The bank server does not verify the client's card credential before executing privileged actions. While the encrypted channel requires the shared secret (channel authentication), the server only validates the auth-file name and that card-file is a syntactically valid filename; it never reads or verifies the card file contents. The client (atm) enforces card-file checks locally before sending requests, but the server trusts the client-supplied arguments. Therefore a client that can produce correctly encrypted messages (i.e., has the channel key) but does not possess/verify the card credential can still cause privileged effects on the server — an unauthenticated client can trigger privileged actions.
EVIDENCE:
- Server decrypts and accepts only properly encrypted messages (channel authentication), but only reports a decrypt error; it does not verify card contents on the server side: [/repo/bank:408-416] (decrypt and error handling).
- Server argument validation checks that auth_file equals the server's auth filename and that card_file is syntactically valid, but it does not open or verify the card file contents: [/repo/bank:169-193] (are_valid_args checks) and [/repo/bank:182-186] (card_file check only validates filename format).
- Server operation handlers perform privileged actions (create/deposit/withdraw/get) based solely on the parsed args and add_entry/balance state; they do not verify any client-side credential or card contents before performing the action: [/repo/bank:215-241] (operation_n and operation_d) and [/repo/bank:244-273] (operation_w and operation_g).
- The client enforces card-file-based authentication locally (it reads the card file and checks its contents match generate_hash(account) before sending requests). This shows authentication is only enforced client-side: [/repo/atm:458-466] (read card file) and [/repo/atm:461-465] (card file contents compared to generate_hash(account)).

Because server-side verification of the credential is missing, requests with missing/failed credentials can still trigger privileged effects if the attacker can produce correctly encrypted messages (i.e., knows the channel key). This satisfies the failing condition "Unauthenticated client".

summary='**Analyzing Ruby precedence**\n\nIn Ruby, the unary \'!\' operator has higher precedence than \'==\'. This means that the expression `!client_input[\'input\'][-2] == \'message_id\'` actually evaluates as `(!client_input[\'input\'][-2]) == \'message_id\'`, which compares a boolean to a string. The comparison fails, so the intended check on the second-to-last element isn’t working. Instead, it should be `client_input[\'input\'][-2] != \'message_id\'` or `!(client_input[\'input\'][-2] == \'message_id\')` to operate correctly. The existing logic ultimately fails to check for \'message_id\' existence effectively.\n\n**Reviewing argument validation**\n\nIt seems they might allow arrays without a `message_id` to proceed, setting `message_id = client_input[\'input\'].last`, which could be nil. Later, `are_valid_args?` checks `is_valid_message_id?(args[:message_id])`, but if `message_id` is nil, it would raise a NoMethodError when trying to access `message_id.length`. The check in `are_valid_args?` confirms if `args[:message_id]` is nil, returning false, which could be a protective measure against invalid arguments. However, there\'s another potential bug in the args extraction that needs attention.\n\n**Examining array index issues**\n\nRuby arrays use a 0 to count-1 indexing system. If `index + 1` equals count, trying to access `[count]` returns nil, but the check incorrectly uses `<= count` instead of `< count`. This could assign nil to args if the last key exists without a value. Luckily, `are_valid_args?` checks for the existence of `args[:operation]` and mostly handles these cases. However, there\'s a risk with the `decrypt` implementation if `text` is nil. The call to decrypt might lead to a NoMethodError, but that\'s caught safely with rescue. Now to evaluate the ATM side next.\n\n**Assessing decryption error handling**\n\nThe decryption process is set up to rescue only `OpenSSL::Cipher::CipherError`, but it may raise other exceptions like a NoMethodError if `raw_result` is nil. Since `sock.read` can return nil on EOF, this could become an issue. However, there\'s an outer rescue that catches all errors from the TCP block, exiting with `PROTOCOL_EXIT_CODE`. The structure includes a timeout block, and general errors are appropriately managed. The inner rescue for decrypt only handles `CipherError`, which seems a bit narrow, but the outer one takes care of broader issues. The use of `return` in the decryption rescue might be redundant.\n\n**Exploring edge cases in exception handling**\n\nIn the bank\'s code, there\'s a structure allowing it to catch `Timeout::Error`, but uncaught exceptions like `NoMethodError` could still arise if `raw_result` is nil. While there are logical bugs, most seem managed through checks and rescues. Potential issues like improper handling in `args` extraction could create risks, but the current structure mostly protects against crashes. VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The protocol uses a nonce field but does not enforce freshness: nonces are neither validated nor recorded on receipt, and the sender increments a uint64 nonce without bounding/wraparound checks. This lacks replay protection and allows nonce reuse/overflow.
EVIDENCE:
- Nonce generation and global counter: [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:35] declares nextNonce; [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:177-181] writes the nonce into the secretbox, packs it into the Packet, and increments nextNonce without bounds or overflow handling:
  - [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:35] var nextNonce uint64 = 1337
  - [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:177-181] byteOrder.PutUint64(nonce[:], nextNonce); ... var packet = Packet{Size: uint64(len(box)), Nonce: nextNonce}; nextNonce++
- No freshness validation on receive: [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:151-169] shows readMessage reads packet.Nonce and uses it only to construct the NaCl nonce for decryption; there is no check that the nonce is within an expected window, unique, or previously unseen. The code accepts any packet whose secretbox decryption succeeds:
  - [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:151-156] binary.Read(reader, byteOrder, &packet)
  - [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:163-166] byteOrder.PutUint64(nonce[:], packet.Nonce); msg, valid := secretbox.Open(...); if !valid { err = errors.New("Invalid message received") }

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: All runtime ATM<->bank messages that influence control flow or state are protected with a keyed authenticated-encryption (NaCl secretbox) and are verified on all acceptance paths. The code verifies incoming boxes with secretbox.Open and rejects (returns error) on invalid MACs; it only processes client requests (which mutate state) after successful read/verification. All outgoing responses (including normal SUCCESS/FAILURE responses) are sent via secretbox.Seal using the same sharedSecret key. No code path accepts or acts on an attacker-controlled message without MAC verification.
EVIDENCE:
- Protocol uses NaCl secretbox (keyed authenticated encryption): [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:7-9]
- Incoming messages are decrypted and authenticated with secretbox.Open; invalid authentication returns an error (so message is rejected): [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:151-169]
- Outgoing messages are sealed (encrypted + MAC) with secretbox.Seal before sending: [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:173-186]
- The bank only processes requests after reading/verifying the client message and checking validity; state-changing handler is called only after that: [/repo/src/main/bank.go:49-66]
- The ATM reads and verifies server messages before acting on them (checks validServerMsg and acts only on SUCCESS): [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:65-83] and [/repo/src/main/atm.go:39-46]
- Key material is established/shared via an auth file: bank generates it with rand.Read into sharedSecret [/repo/src/main/bank.go:68-74] and ATM reads it from disk and copies into sharedSecret [/repo/src/main/atm.go:24-27] (with length check: [/repo/src/main/atm.go:59-63]).

These artifacts show (1) a keyed AEAD is used (not a bare/unkeyed MAC), (2) verification happens at read time and errors are returned on invalid MACs, and (3) state-changing code paths are only reached after successful read/verification. No evidence of unauthenticated acceptance, unkeyed MACs, or skipping MAC checks on return/error paths was found.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The server's observable packet Size (sent unencrypted in the Packet header) is directly correlated with whether the response includes a balance and with the balance magnitude. Server serialization encodes StatusCode (1 byte) + an 8-byte balance-word-count + 8 bytes per big.Word of balance. A successful GET returns the balance (non-nil) while failures or non-GET responses usually send a nil balance, producing different cleartext message lengths which result in different packet sizes on the wire. This allows a man-in-the-middle to distinguish success vs failure and infer balance magnitude from packet sizes.
EVIDENCE: 
- Message/packet format: [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:15-18] (Packet struct) and [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:151-169] (readMessage) and [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:173-187] (sendMessage). The Packet header (Size, Nonce) is written in clear and thus reveals ciphertext length.
- Server serialization of responses: [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:100-114] (sendServerMsg) — writes StatusCode (1 byte), then writeUint64(len(balanceBits)) (8 bytes), then writeWords(balance) which emits 8 bytes per word ([/repo/src/main/protocol.go:144-147]).
- Server deserialization (shows the symmetric format): [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:70-81] (readServerMsg) — reads StatusCode and a uint64 balance length then reads that many words into the balance.
- Account GET returns a balance on success and bank sends this balance: [/repo/src/main/accounts.go:90-97] (accountGet returning SUCCESS, balance) and [/repo/src/main/bank.go:58-61] (handleRequest calling sendServerMsg with the returned balance).
- Artifact with worked-out byte counts and explanation: /evidence/artifacts/leak_evidence.txt (created). This shows concrete packet lengths (e.g., 41 bytes vs 49 bytes on the wire for nil vs 1-word balance) and explains how the length grows by 8 bytes per big.Word.

Because the Size field and packet header are unprotected and the server deterministically encodes presence/size of the balance into message length, the repository fails the test: an attacker can use observable metadata (packet sizes) to infer account balance existence and magnitude.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: Static and control-flow inspection show that the server only executes privileged account operations when (1) the wire message is successfully authenticated/decrypted (secretbox.Open) and (2) the client-supplied credential (card) is present and verified via isAuthorized (card equality) before any account state-changing functions run. Messages failing authentication or missing/invalid credentials are rejected and do not trigger account effects.

EVIDENCE:
- Channel authentication check: the server decrypts & authenticates each packet and returns an error when verification fails: [repo/src/main/protocol.go:151-169] (secretbox.Open -> if !valid { err = errors.New("Invalid message received") }).
- Error handling prevents processing unauthenticated messages: readClientMsg is called by handleRequest and any returned error is passed to bankEnsure which prints a protocol error and panics (the panic is recovered per-connection), so the request is not processed: [repo/src/main/bank.go:49-56] (handleRequest calling readClientMsg and only proceeding on success) and [repo/src/main/util.go:15-21] (bankEnsure behaviour).
- Credential presence and verification before privileged actions: handleAccountRequest only calls account operations when isAuthorized(...) is true; isAuthorized allows RequestNew (account creation) or otherwise requires account != nil && bytes.Equal(account.card, card): [repo/src/main/accounts.go:24-33] and [repo/src/main/accounts.go:47-50]. Thus deposit/withdraw/get require the provided card to match the stored card.
- Account-operation implementations only modify state when preconditions are met (e.g., account != nil, sufficient balance, or minimum new-account balance): [repo/src/main/accounts.go:53-63] (accountNew), [repo/src/main/accounts.go:66-74] (accountDeposit), [repo/src/main/accounts.go:78-86] (accountWithdraw), [repo/src/main/accounts.go:90-97] (accountGet).

Notes / scope: Replay/tampering of previously authenticated traffic is out of scope per the test. I did static code analysis; runtime verification was not performed because the environment lacks the Go toolchain (go was not available). The code paths and checks cited above provide direct, verifiable evidence that unauthenticated clients (messages failing secretbox verification) and requests with missing/incorrect card credentials cannot cause privileged account effects.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The client-side message parsing (readServerMsg) uses an attacker-controlled length field to allocate a slice without bounds checking, which can cause a runtime panic (makeslice: len out of range / OOM). Such a panic is not caught by the ATM client (no recover), so a malicious server can crash the client. This violates the requirement that attacker-influenced runtime interactions must not throw uncaught exceptions impacting protocol integrity.

EVIDENCE:
- Unchecked length -> allocation:
  - [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:73-77] shows readServerMsg reads balanceLen from the (decrypted) message and immediately does `var balance = make([]big.Word, balanceLen)` with no bounds check.
    - [/repo/src/main/protocol.go:73-77] (lines: 73: // Balance; 74: balanceLen, err := readUint64(reader); 75: if err != nil { return }; 76: var balance = make([]big.Word, balanceLen); 77: err = readWords(reader, balance))

- Client does not recover from panics:
  - [/repo/src/main/atm.go:39-41] shows the ATM calls readServerMsg wrapped by atmEnsure, which only checks returned errors; a runtime panic occurring inside readServerMsg will not be converted into an error and will crash the client.
    - [/repo/src/main/atm.go:39-41] (atmEnsure(sendClientMsg...), atmEnsure(readServerMsg(...)))

- Demonstration that an oversized length allocation panics at runtime:
  - Proof-of-concept program that mirrors the vulnerable allocation was run and produced a runtime panic (makeslice: len out of range).
    - Program saved at: /repo/evidence_poc/poc.go
    - Runtime output (showing the panic) saved at: /repo/evidence/artifacts/poc_run.txt
    - Contents of the run log (excerpt):
      balanceLen=1152921504606846976
      panic: runtime error: makeslice: len out of range

- Server-side protections (context):
  - The server-side handler recovers from panics in per-connection goroutines ([/repo/src/main/bank.go:49-52] defer func() { conn.Close(); recover() }()), and bankEnsure panics on error ([/repo/src/main/util.go:15-20]). This means some server-side panics are contained, but the client-side parsing lacks such protection.

Taken together, these artifacts show a reachable attacker-influenced field (balanceLen in a server message) is used unchecked to allocate memory, resulting in an uncaught runtime panic on the ATM client. Therefore the test fails.

If you want, I can produce a networked proof-of-concept that runs the ATM binary and a malicious server to crash it, but that requires generating/placing a matching auth file (shared secret) for the ATM so it accepts and decrypts the malicious response; the static evidence plus the standalone makeslice POC is already sufficient to conclude FAIL.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository generates card secrets with a cryptographically secure RNG (crypto/rand) when creating a new card and does not derive card values deterministically from public identifiers such as the account name. There is no code that hashes or computes the card from the account name. The card file name is derived from the account name, but the card contents themselves are produced by random bytes at creation.
EVIDENCE: 
- Card generation uses crypto/rand.Read to fill a CARD_LEN byte slice when creating a new card: [/workdir/repo/src/main/atm.go:67-71].
- The code that loads an existing card file only reads the raw bytes; it does not compute the card from the account name: [/workdir/repo/src/main/atm.go:76-80] and the default card filename is account + ".card": [/workdir/repo/src/main/args.go:96-104].
- The server authorizes requests by comparing the provided card bytes with the stored card bytes (bytewise equality), i.e. it uses the card as a secret token rather than deriving it from the account name: [/workdir/repo/src/main/accounts.go:47-50].
- CARD_LEN is defined as 16 bytes, confirming the card is a fixed-length secret: [/workdir/repo/src/main/constants.go:40].
- There is no import or use of hashing libraries (e.g. crypto/sha*, md5) to derive a card from the account name anywhere in the source; card material is only produced via crypto/rand.Read (atm) or read from disk.

Notes / caveats:
- If an operator places a non-random (predictable) card file on disk before the ATM performs Account New, the code will accept it; this is an operational risk but not a code defect in generation. The repository itself creates cards using a secure RNG.
- Network confidentiality depends on the shared auth secret and secretbox usage; this assessment is limited to whether card values are random / not deterministically derived.

All cited files exist in the repository at the stated paths and line ranges.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: All network payload bytes that carry sensitive fields (account, card, operation, value, balance, etc.) are sent only after being encrypted by CommonUtils.encrypt and are received and decrypted by CommonUtils.decrypt on the other side. There is no code path that writes those sensitive fields in plaintext to the socket; the only on-the-wire plaintext data is a 4-byte length prefix (written via writeInt), which does not contain sensitive account data.

EVIDENCE:
- Atm constructs the sensitive request string and immediately encrypts it before sending:
  - [/repo/Atm.java:212-221] (createBankQuerry builds outString containing account, card, operation, value and calls CommonUtils.encrypt on padding + outString + padding)
  - [/repo/Atm.java:178-181] (the encrypted outputdata is written to the socket via dos.writeInt(...) and dos.write(outputdata,...))

- Bank receives bytes from the network and immediately decrypts them before parsing the sensitive fields:
  - [/repo/Bank.java:275-283] (processInput calls CommonUtils.decrypt on theInput and then splits and uses the decrypted string to set transaction fields)
  - [/repo/Bank.java:288-290] (response JSON containing sensitive fields is encrypted with CommonUtils.encrypt before being written back to the socket)

- The encryption/decryption implementation used for the on-wire payloads is in CommonUtils and wraps the entire payload (no partial/plaintext fields):
  - [/repo/CommonUtils.java:141-147] (encrypt uses RC4 with the provided key over the entire string)
  - [/repo/CommonUtils.java:150-156] (decrypt likewise runs RC4 decrypt and returns the full plaintext string)
  - [/repo/CommonUtils.java:7-50] (RC4 implementation which is used to transform the full payload bytes)

Notes:
- The code sends a 4-byte length prefix (DataOutputStream.writeInt) in plaintext; this does not contain account/balance/etc. and is not considered sensitive by the test description. All sensitive data bytes are included inside the encrypted ciphertext written immediately after the length.
- This verdict concerns whether on-wire sensitive bytes are encrypted. It does not assess cryptographic strength (RC4 is considered weak) because the test only requires that sensitive fields are not sent in plaintext.

Given the static and dynamic code paths shown above, the repository satisfies the test requirement that no plaintext (or partially-plaintext) sensitive fields are transmitted between ATM and Bank.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository uses an RC4 stream cipher keyed only by a static secret that is generated once by the Bank and stored in bank.auth. That same secret is read by the ATM and reused for all encryptions/decryptions. There is no per-message IV/nonce or per-message key derivation: the RC4 key (seed) is fixed across all runtime messages, so the IV/seed is not fresh per-message.
EVIDENCE:
- /workdir/repo/CommonUtils.java:12-21 shows RC4 KSA uses only the provided key bytes (no IV): the constructor copies key bytes into T and initializes S with them.
  [/workdir/repo/CommonUtils.java:12-21]
- /workdir/repo/CommonUtils.java:32-46 shows RC4 keystream generation (encrypt) uses only the internal state initialized from the key; there is no IV mixing per-encryption. [/workdir/repo/CommonUtils.java:32-46]
- /workdir/repo/CommonUtils.java:141-148 shows CommonUtils.encrypt constructs a new RC4 instance with the provided bkey (the only seed for the cipher): RC4 rc4 = new RC4(bkey); return rc4.encrypt(...). There is no IV parameter. [/workdir/repo/CommonUtils.java:141-148]
- /workdir/repo/Bank.java:76-81 shows the Bank generates a single random secret once (SecureRandom.nextBytes(secret)) and writes it to the auth file. This is a one-time secret used as the cipher key. [/workdir/repo/Bank.java:76-81]
- /workdir/repo/Bank.java:26-27 declares the secret byte[] that is reused by the server for decrypt/encrypt operations. [/workdir/repo/Bank.java:26-27]
- /workdir/repo/Bank.java:275-291 shows processInput decrypts and encrypts messages via CommonUtils.decrypt/encrypt using that secret (no IV/nonce): decrypt(theInput, secret) and later encrypt(..., secret). [/workdir/repo/Bank.java:275-291]
- /workdir/repo/Atm.java:123-126 shows the ATM reads the same secret from the auth file into its secret array (FileInputStream.read(secret,...)). [/workdir/repo/Atm.java:123-126]
- /workdir/repo/Atm.java:190-191 and 212-221 show the ATM uses CommonUtils.decrypt(..., secret) and CommonUtils.encrypt(..., secret) for network messages, again passing the same secret as the only seed. [/workdir/repo/Atm.java:190-191] [/workdir/repo/Atm.java:212-221]
Notes: The code adds variable-length zero-byte padding using java.util.Random to change message lengths, but that does not introduce a per-message IV or change the cipher key/seed. Therefore the cipher keystream is derived solely from the fixed secret and so the IV/seed is effectively constant across encryptions.

Because the test requires the IV/seed to be per-message fresh, and this repository uses a fixed key/seed for all messages, the test FAILs.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The ATM<->Bank messages are only symmetrically encrypted (RC4) and there is no keyed message-authentication tag generation or verification anywhere. The bank accepts and processes decrypted messages (including returning responses and committing state) without any separate MAC verification; error and return paths do not perform any MAC checks.
EVIDENCE: 
- Message creation at ATM uses only symmetric encryption with the shared secret: [repo/Atm.java:212-221] shows createBankQuerry() builds the plaintext and calls CommonUtils.encrypt(..., secret).
- The encryption primitive is RC4 (a stream cipher) and there is no MAC generation in CommonUtils: [repo/CommonUtils.java:7-16] (RC4 constructor) and [repo/CommonUtils.java:141-156] (encrypt/decrypt) implement RC4-based encrypt/decrypt, not a MAC/HMAC/tag.
- The bank decrypts and immediately parses the plaintext without any MAC verification: [repo/Bank.java:275-283] (processInput) calls CommonUtils.decrypt(theInput, secret) and then sets the transaction from the parsed fields.
- The server thread accepts the processed transaction and sends a response and later writes to the database without any MAC check on the input or on error/return paths: [repo/Bank.java:232-266] (BankServerThread.start) shows reading input, calling processInput, sending output, then calling transaction.writeToDatabase(); error handling at [repo/Bank.java:267-270] simply cancels and prints "protocol_error" without any verification.
- No MAC/HMAC/tag/verify/signature functions or references were found in the repository (search for keywords such as "mac", "hmac", "tag", "verify", "signature" returned no matches).

Because acceptance (processing and committing state) is not conditioned on verifying a keyed authentication tag, and no MAC checks exist on return or error paths, this fails the test.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The protocol leaks predictable length-based metadata (and even sends the payload length in clear). The server and client both prepend/write the exact payload length as a 4-byte integer, and the encrypted response length depends directly on the JSON response contents ("##error##" vs JSON with account/balance) with only length-dependent random padding. An attacker observing message lengths (or the explicit length field) can distinguish error vs successful responses and infer account/balance-related information.
EVIDENCE: 
- Clear-text length field is written/read by client and server: [repo/Atm.java:178-181] (dos.writeInt(outputdata.length); dos.write(...)) and [repo/Atm.java:184-188] (int len = dis.readInt(); ...). Server writes the response length at [repo/Bank.java:255-258] (dos.writeInt(outputdata.length); dos.write(...)). These 4-byte length headers are observable by a network attacker.
- Server response body depends on account/balance and is variable-length JSON when successful versus the fixed error marker when failing: the error default is set at [repo/Bank.java:111] (private String json = "##error##";) and successful balance response builds variable-length JSON at [repo/Bank.java:155-160] (json = "{\"account\":\"" + accountName + "\",\"balance\":" + longToStr(account.getBalance()) + "}"). That JSON length varies with account name and balance digits.
- Both client and server add length-dependent random padding (not constant-length), so the final ciphertext length is correlated with the underlying message length: client constructs its query with padding based on message length at [repo/Atm.java:216-219] (int ml = outString.length(); ... new String(new byte[random.nextInt(ml/2)]) + outString + new String(new byte[random.nextInt(ml/2)])). Server similarly pads responses at [repo/Bank.java:285-289] (int ml = outString.length(); ... new String(new byte[random.nextInt(ml/2)]) + outString + new String(new byte[random.nextInt(ml/2)])). Because the random padding bounds depend on ml, ciphertext length distributions differ by underlying message length.
- Encryption implementation (RC4) is in [repo/CommonUtils.java:141-157], but encryption strength is out-of-scope per the test. The presence of explicit length headers and length-dependent padding is sufficient evidence of metadata leakage.

Together, these show a passive observer can measure the explicit length header or ciphertext length and distinguish errors vs successful responses and infer message-dependent data (account name/balance). Therefore the test fails.

- Privileged effects (database changes) are only applied if the transaction was marked valid: [/repo/Bank.java:168-186] (writeToDatabase applies changes only when valid is true and then prints the JSON). If an exception occurs the transaction is cancelled and no change is persisted: [/repo/Bank.java:264-270] (after exception, transaction.cancel() and "protocol_error").
- Encryption / decryption implementation (RC4) showing that a shared secret is required to produce valid plaintext: [/repo/CommonUtils.java:141-156] (encrypt/decrypt using RC4 with bkey).

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: I found no evidence of reachable, attacker-influenced runtime interactions that cause uncaught exceptions which would break protocol integrity. Input-size checks are present on both client and server before allocating buffers; parsing-related exceptions (e.g., malformed messages or parsing errors) are caught and lead to a controlled protocol_error handling path and transaction rollback. There are a few places that index into split arrays without an explicit length check, but these exceptions would be thrown inside the server processing and are caught by the surrounding try/catch so they do not propagate uncaught or leave the server in an inconsistent committed state.

EVIDENCE:
- Server verifies incoming message length and reads exact bytes: [/repo/Bank.java:244-251] (Server reads int len, checks "if (len > 0 && len < 1024)" and then dis.readFully(inputdata)).
- Client verifies reply length and reads exact bytes: [/repo/Atm.java:184-188] (Client reads len and checks "if (len > 0 && len < 1024)" and then dis.readFully(inputdata)).
- Server processes input (decryption + split) and accesses split parts without explicit length checks: [/repo/Bank.java:275-283] (CommonUtils.decrypt(...) then split and usages strs[2], strs[0], strs[1], strs[3]). This is a potential source of ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for malformed inputs, but see next point.
- All server-side exceptions during a connection are caught and handled: [/repo/Bank.java:236-271] (the entire connection handling is in a try-with-resources; any Exception triggers transaction.cancel() and prints "protocol_error"; resources are closed by try-with-resources). Specifically the catch block is at [/repo/Bank.java:267-270].
- Transaction rollback/cancel ensures no partial commit after protocol errors: [/repo/Bank.java:190-195] (Transaction.cancel removes new accounts created by a failed transaction). Also final commit is only done after successful processing: [/repo/Bank.java:264-266] (transaction.writeToDatabase() called only after response sent and no exception thrown).
- Client-side exceptions are also caught and handled (remove created card file on error and exit with code): [/repo/Atm.java:203-208] (catch block that deletes card file for operation 'n' and exits). Also client creation of messages and file reads are guarded by checks earlier in init (file existence, name validation). Examples: reading secret file [/repo/Atm.java:123-129] and card file logic [/repo/Atm.java:136-149].

Notes on why this satisfies the test conditions:
- "Uncaught exception": I found no code paths where an exception thrown during a network-handling interaction would be left uncaught. Exceptions in BankServerThread.start (which encloses the network interaction and processing) are caught and result in a controlled error path.
- "Do not check packet size": Both server and client check the 4-byte length prefix and enforce 0 < len < 1024 before allocating and reading. See citations above.
- "Disrupted state between server and client": The server uses try-with-resources to ensure sockets are closed on error; transaction changes are only written to the in-memory database after response send; on exception the transaction is canceled. This prevents inconsistent commits.
- "Insufficient error checking with packet extension": While there is a location where split() array indices are used without checking length [/repo/Bank.java:279-281], that exception is caught at the connection level and results in controlled cancellation and protocol_error rather than a crash or unhandled exception.

If you want, I can produce a small test harness that sends malformed or truncated messages to the server and demonstrate, with logs, that the server responds with the protocol_error path and that no uncaught exceptions crash the JVM or leave inconsistent state. That would provide runtime traces to corroborate the static evidence above.

- repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Encryption.cs: shows the no-arg constructor generating IV/Key once and storing them in _IV/_Key (lines 21-31), and the Encrypt/Decrypt methods re-using _IV for every encryption/decryption (lines 61-66 and 80-86): [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Encryption.cs:21-33], [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Encryption.cs:61-66], [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Encryption.cs:80-86].
- repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Encryption.cs: shows same pattern on the Bank side — constructor generates and stores IV/Key once (lines 20-30) and Encrypt/Decrypt set aes.IV = _IV (lines 55-58 and 76-80). This indicates Bank sends/receives ciphertexts using the same stored IV across messages: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Encryption.cs:20-31], [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Encryption.cs:55-58], [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Encryption.cs:76-80].
- repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Program.cs: the Bank creates a single Encryption instance at startup and writes the key to bank.auth: new Encryption() is constructed at program scope (line 19) and GetKey() is written to the auth file (lines 19 and 65): [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Program.cs:19-19], [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Program.cs:65-67]. That single Encryption instance is passed to the Bank/BankServer and used for all messages.
- repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Program.cs: the ATM reads the written auth file and constructs an Encryption from it once (line 116-118), so the ATM side also uses a fixed IV/key loaded once rather than a fresh IV per message: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Program.cs:116-118].
- repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/ATMClient.cs: the client uses the same _Crypto.Encrypt() for sending messages (lines 137-142), proving runtime messages are encrypted with that fixed instance: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/ATMClient.cs:137-142].
- repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/BankServer.cs: BankServer.Send encrypts outgoing messages with _Crypto.Encrypt(...) before sending (lines 222-227), again showing the server re-uses its stored IV for outgoing messages: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/BankServer.cs:222-227].

These code locations demonstrate that the IV is generated or loaded once per Encryption instance and re-used for every encryption call, so IV/seed is not per-message fresh. Therefore the test fails (Fixed IV / Fixed IV seed).

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The ATM↔Bank protocol contains no explicit freshness (nonce/timestamp) carried in requests or responses and receivers do not validate freshness. The client computes a deterministic pinHash based only on operation/account/pin and sends XML; the server decrypts and accepts based on the hash without any nonce/timestamp checks. Although BankServer records a receive timestamp in a Packet object, that timestamp is never used to enforce freshness or to prevent replays.
EVIDENCE: 
- ATM computes the pinHash from only operation, account and pin, then adds it to the XML and sends the message: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Program.cs:163-169] (content="..." then hash computed and added as pinHash, then _Client.Send(protocol.ToString())). See lines 163-166 where content and hash are built and the pinHash attribute is added, and line 169 where the protocol is sent.
- Server decrypts and delivers the message to processing without any freshness checks: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/BankServer.cs:132-139] (Packet created with DateTime.Now and content decrypted, then OnMessage invoked). There is no validation of any nonce/timestamp before accepting the message.
- Packet stores a Timestamp but that value is never used elsewhere in the code (no checks or recording to prevent reuse): [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/BankServer.cs:152-162]. The Timestamp field exists but is not referenced for acceptance logic.
- Authentication on the server side is purely a hash comparison derived from fixed inputs (operation, account, stored pin) — no nonce/timestamp is part of authentication: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Account.cs:86-96] (ValidatePin only formats "{operation} - {account} - {pin}" and SHA256s it).
- No code constructs, propagates, checks, bounds, or records nonces/timestamps in request/response paths anywhere in the repo (searched repository for "nonce", "timestamp", "fresh" and found no protocol usage; the only Timestamp is the Packet.Timestamp which is unused). (Search evidence: repository-wide inspection.)

Because the protocol does not carry or validate freshness values, it fails the test (replay protection / freshness requirements). The precise failing conditions observed include: "No nonce used", "Nonce not checked on receive", and "Nonces not recorded" as defined by the test.

If you want, I can produce a small patch that adds a nonce/timestamp attribute to the XML protocol, makes the ATM include it, and instruments the Bank to check and record nonces to prevent reuse (including bounding timestamp windows).

metadata.test_description: For every reachable security-relevant request/response exchange, the protocol uses an explicit freshness value (nonce/timestamp) when required, and receivers enforce freshness on all acceptance paths by validating it on receipt (including return/error paths), bounding it (no overflow / overly-large windows), and tracking it to prevent reuse; additionally, any freshness carried in responses that is relied upon by the protocol is also checked. Fails iff: `No nonce used`, `Nonce not checked on receive`, `Nonces not checked`, `Nonces not recorded`, `Response value nonce not checked`, `Nonce overflows`, `Timestamp window too large for nonce`, `Ignore check failure`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The ATM<->Bank protocol uses only symmetric encryption (AES) for confidentiality and performs no keyed message-authentication (no MAC/HMAC/signature) on any incoming or outgoing messages. Messages are decrypted and directly parsed/executed to update state (Create/Withdraw/Deposit) without any MAC verification on success or error/return paths.

EVIDENCE:
- Bank receives, decrypts and dispatches messages without any MAC verification: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/BankServer.cs:129-139] shows the code extracting the "<EOF>"-stripped payload and calling _Crypto.Decrypt(...) then OnMessage(...).
- Bank processes decrypted messages and updates state (transactions) without checking any authentication tag: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Bank.cs:72-81] (handling Transaction -> ProcessATM) and [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Bank.cs:124-151] (ProcessATM executes Create/Withdraw/Deposit using values from the parsed XML).
- Bank sends responses by encrypting plaintext only (no MAC on return): [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/BankServer.cs:200-207] (Send method uses _Crypto.Encrypt(message) + "<EOF>").
- The Encryption implementations use AES Encrypt/Decrypt only and do not compute or verify any MAC/HMAC: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Encryption.cs:51-70] (Encrypt) and [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Encryption.cs:74-88] (Decrypt); [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Encryption.cs:56-76] (Encrypt) and [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Encryption.cs:80-94] (Decrypt).
- ATM client likewise decrypts received data and passes it to handlers without MAC verification: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/ATMClient.cs:105-113] (Decrypt then OnMessage).

Because no keyed MAC computation or verification appears anywhere on message receipt or on responses, the test fails under the stated criteria ("No MAC", "No MAC on return").

Notes for reproduction/verification: the cited source lines exist in the repository at the given paths and show the exact use of Encrypt/Decrypt and the absence of any MAC/HMAC/signature checks.

metadata.test_description: For every reachable attacker-controllable atm<->bank runtime message that can influence control flow or state, acceptance is conditioned on verifying a keyed message-authentication tag, and that verification is enforced on all acceptance paths (including return/error paths). Fails iff: `No MAC`, `No MAC on return`, `Unkeyed MAC`, `MAC not checked for error response`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The server sends short fixed failure strings ("255") on error and full JSON responses (including account name and numeric balance) on success. These are encrypted and base64-encoded but their ciphertext/base64 lengths differ deterministically with the plaintext length. An on-path observer can therefore distinguish fail vs success (and infer balance magnitude digits) from message length/connection behavior. The code also exposes connection-level metadata (socket disconnects and explicit "protocol_error" behavior). 

EVIDENCE:
1) Server sends failure code "255" on exception: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Bank.cs:72-86] (see line 85: _Server.Send(state.Socket, "255");). This shows a short predictable failure plaintext is returned.

2) Successful operations return JSON containing account name and balance: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/ProcessATM and Account.cs:124-156, /repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Account.cs:76-84]. In particular, Account.GetBalance returns JSON with the account and numeric balance: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Account.cs:78-84] (return String.Format(_ReturnJSON, AccountName, "balance", _Balance);), and _ReturnJSON shows the exact format: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Account.cs:16-17]. ProcessATM returns that JSON to be sent: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Bank.cs:75-81 and 153-156].

3) Responses are encrypted then base64-encoded and sent verbatim (so ciphertext length depends on plaintext length): [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Encryption.cs:51-70] (Encrypt returns Convert.ToBase64String(ms.ToArray());) and [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/BankServer.cs:222-229] (Send builds data = _Crypto.Encrypt(message) + "<EOF>" and sends its ASCII bytes). This shows there is no length-hiding or padding beyond standard AES block+base64 encoding.

4) Connection-level metadata and explicit disconnects are observable: BankServer timer case prints "protocol_error" and closes/disconnects the socket: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/BankServer.cs:212-219] (Console.WriteLine("protocol_error"); _socket.Disconnect(true); _socket.Close();). Bank also writes protocol_error on timeout in [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Bank.cs:28-41]. These behaviors leak observable connection events.

5) Reproducible encryption-length examples (demonstrating that small plaintexts like "255" produce much shorter base64 ciphertexts than JSON responses and that different balances change plaintext length and thus ciphertext length) were generated and saved: [/evidence/artifacts/encryption_length_examples.txt]. Example lines (excerpt):
   - fail: plaintext_len=3, b64_len=24
   - success_small: plaintext_len=33, b64_len=64
   - success_medium: plaintext_len=34, b64_len=64
   - success_large: plaintext_len=37, b64_len=64

   File path: /evidence/artifacts/encryption_length_examples.txt

Explanation of why this fails the test case:
- The test checks whether an on-path attacker can use observable metadata (message length / connection metadata) to derive an account's name or balance. Here, success responses include the account name and numeric balance in the plaintext JSON; failure responses are a short fixed string "255". After encryption and base64, ciphertext lengths remain correlated with plaintext length (AES/CBC with PKCS#7 padding + base64 does not obfuscate length sufficiently). Therefore an attacker distinguishing message lengths can infer whether the transaction succeeded, and by observing varying ciphertext lengths across balances (number of digits) can distinguish approximate balance magnitude. The server also emits observable connection events (protocol_error + disconnect) that further leak information.

Conclusion: The repository fails the test because it produces predictable/observable differences in response length and connection behavior that leak account existence and balance information to a man-in-the-middle observer.

metadata.test_description: A man in the middle attacker cannot use observable metadata to derive either an account's name or balance. For instance, if message length differs between fail and success, then it may be possible to derive account balance. (Lack of encryption is out of scope for this property as this only pertains to message length or connection metadata.) Fails iff: `Predictable fail/success response length`, `Do not protect connection metadata`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The code enforces both channel-level authentication (messages must decrypt with the bank's symmetric key) and per-request credential verification (pinHash checked on every privileged operation). Invalid/missing credentials cause ValidatePin to throw and exceptions are caught upstream, preventing any privileged state change.
EVIDENCE:
- Incoming messages are decrypted before being processed; if decryption fails the server will not call the message handler: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/BankServer.cs:136-139] (Decrypt + OnMessage call).
- Decryption implementation uses AES and will throw on invalid base64/wrong key, so unauthenticated clients (without the shared key file) cannot produce a valid decrypted payload: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Encryption.cs:74-88].
- Privileged operations (Create, Withdraw, Deposit, Get) require a pinHash attribute and are dispatched via ProcessATM which reads pinHash from the request: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Bank.cs:124-129,130-137,139-148].
- Each Account operation calls ValidatePin, which computes the server-side hash and throws on mismatch: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Account.cs:47-51,65-69,78-83,86-96]. Any thrown exception prevents the operation from completing.
- Exceptions from ProcessATM are caught at the message handling layer and result in an error response ("255") rather than applying effects: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Bank.cs:72-86].

These code paths together show that (1) a client must have the shared key (the channel/authentication) to send a decryptable request, and (2) each privileged request must include a correct pinHash which is verified server-side; missing or incorrect credentials produce exceptions and no privileged effect. Therefore the repository satisfies the test.

metadata.test_description: For every privileged-action execution event, the action executes only if the communication channel is authenticated and the request includes credentials that are present and verified; requests with missing/failed credentials cannot trigger privileged effects. (Replay/tampering of previously authenticated traffic is out of scope for this property.) Fails iff: `Unauthenticated client`.

For every reachable attacker-influenced runtime interaction, the implementation does not throw uncaught exceptions impacting the integrity of the protocol (e.g. performing size dependent operations without verifying message size resulting in a crash). Fails iff: `Uncaught exception`, `Do not check packet size`, `Disrupted state between server and client`, `Insufficient error checking with packet extension`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The card "secret" is a 4-digit PIN generated with System.Random (low entropy, guessable). The card file stores the account and this 4-digit PIN ("account - pin") encrypted, so the effective secret protecting authorization is only 10,000 possibilities and can be brute-forced. This violates the requirement that card values be high-entropy and not deterministically derived.
EVIDENCE: 
- PIN generation and card file contents (low-entropy numeric PIN written to card): [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Program.cs:143-155] (string pin = new Random().Next(9999).ToString().PadLeft(4, '0'); content = account + " - " + pin; File.WriteAllText(cardFile, encrypted))
- Card read/decrypt path (card file holds encrypted "account - pin" which is later decrypted and used to compute pinHash): [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Program.cs:156-166] (File.ReadAllText(cardFile); content = crypto.Decrypt(encrypted); content = operation + " - " + content; hash = SHA256(...))
- Server-side validation uses the PIN string to compute the SHA256 and compare against the provided pinHash (i.e. the PIN is the secret protecting account ops): [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Account.cs:30-37] (PinCode set from constructor and ValidatePin called) and [/repo/src/BiBiFi/Bank/Account.cs:86-96] (content = "{operation} - {AccountName} - {PinCode}"; serverHash = SHA256(content); compare to provided hash)
- The ATM encrypts/decrypts the card file with AES using the shared auth key (bank.auth), showing the card file is an AES-encrypted serialization of the low-entropy PIN rather than a high-entropy secret: [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Program.cs:114-118] (read _AuthFile and new Encryption(_Authorization)) and [/repo/src/BiBiFi/ATM/Encryption.cs:35-46,56-64] (Encryption constructed from key and Encrypt/Decrypt implementations).

Notes for verification: Because the PIN is only 4 digits (10,000 possibilities) and used directly in the SHA256 computation that authorizes operations, an attacker with the ability to obtain a pinHash (or to attempt authentication if they can submit encrypted messages with the shared key) can brute-force the PIN quickly. The repository therefore FAILS the test.

metadata.test_description: There is no exploitable vulnerability due to guessable/derivable card secrets: any card value used to authorize balance reads/writes is high-entropy and not deterministically derived from public identifiers. This fails if a MITM can guess/compute card secret due to lack of card randomness. Fails iff: `No randomness in card file`, `Card is hash of account name`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: An authentication token (a sensitive runtime value used to authenticate requests) is duplicated inside the encrypted JSON body and also sent in plaintext in an HTTP header (X-ATM-Token). That means a sensitive field from the ATM<->Bank protocol is exposed outside the ciphertext (partial plaintext leak). The account/balance/operation fields are placed in the encrypted body, but the token is transmitted in cleartext.
EVIDENCE: 
- Client side: atm places the token into the payload and then also into an HTTP header before sending the request: [/repo/atm.py:20-24] and [/repo/atm.py:27-31]. These lines show token generation, insertion into params (which are then encoded) and header assignment:
  - [/repo/atm.py:20-24]: token = atm_proto.generate_token(); params["token"] = token; data = atm_proto.encode(params, key)
  - [/repo/atm.py:27-31]: headers include "X-ATM-Token": token

- Encoding: the payload is entirely encoded/encrypted by atm_proto.encode (JSON dumped then AES-CBC encrypt of the whole string): [/repo/lib/atm_proto.py:16-31]. This shows encryption is applied to the whole JSON string prior to sending.

- Server side: the server decodes the request body and then compares the token inside the decrypted payload with the plaintext header value: [/repo/lib/server_handler.py:61-66] and [/repo/lib/server_handler.py:82-95]. These lines show the server does atm_proto.decode(raw, key) and then calls validate_token(data["token"], s.headers["X-ATM-Token"]) which uses the header value in plaintext.

- Additional context: server responses (when present) are sent encrypted in the body using atm_proto.encode: [/repo/lib/server_handler.py:73-76]. This shows responses are encrypted, but it does not mitigate the header leak.

Because an authentication token (sensitive runtime data) is sent in plaintext in the header, the test fails: a sensitive field is not confined to ciphertext and is leaked on the network.

If you consider the token non-sensitive and only care about fields explicitly named (account, balance, operation), those fields are inside the encrypted body (see the encode/decode calls above). However, the protocol explicitly mirrors the token both inside the ciphertext and in a plaintext header, which violates the requirement that no sensitive fields leave any part of the payload unencrypted.

Files and line ranges cited above exist in the repository and can be inspected to reproduce these findings.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The ATM<->Bank protocol uses AES-CBC encryption without an authentication tag (no MAC/HMAC). Both request acceptance and response sending rely on unauthenticated ciphertext and a client-supplied header token comparison; there is no keyed MAC verification on any acceptance path. This violates the requirement that all attacker-controllable messages that influence control flow/state are verified with a keyed MAC on all acceptance paths (including error/return paths).
EVIDENCE:
- No MAC/authentication anywhere in the encoding/decoding routines: [repo/lib/atm_proto.py:16-24] (encrypt/decrypt using AES-CBC with fixed IV, no MAC) and [repo/lib/atm_proto.py:27-31] (encode pads and calls encrypt) and [repo/lib/atm_proto.py:34-46] (decode decrypts and json.loads with no integrity check).
- Server accepts requests based on decoding (unauthenticated) and a token equality check that compares an in-payload token to a header value (both attacker-controllable), with no cryptographic MAC verification: [repo/lib/server_handler.py:61-66] (decode + validate_token) and [repo/lib/server_handler.py:82-95] (validate_token returns True if token equals header; it only logs reused tokens and does not reject them).
- Responses are sent by encoding with atm_proto.encode (also unauthenticated): [repo/lib/server_handler.py:73-76] (send_response then s.wfile.write(atm_proto.encode(out, ...))). The ATM similarly encodes requests and decodes responses without MAC: [repo/atm.py:22-24] (params["token"] added then data = atm_proto.encode(...)) and [repo/atm.py:45-49] (reads response and res_struct = atm_proto.decode(content, key)).
- Practical consequence: AES-CBC without an authentication tag means an attacker who can observe/manipulate network messages can craft or tamper messages to affect server control flow/state without any keyed-MAC verification. The token check compares attacker-controlled header to decrypted token but provides no cryptographic integrity protection.

- [repo/lib/server_handler.py:61-66,73-76,82-95]
- [repo/atm.py:22-24,45-49]

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The server returns an encrypted body on success but no body on failure, and the encryption is deterministic block-padding (no randomized padding). Therefore a passive observer (MITM) can distinguish success vs failure and infer plaintext-length-dependent fields (account name and balance). Connection metadata (response body length / TCP bytes) is left observable.
EVIDENCE: 
- Server only writes a response body when there is an output payload; on error it sends no body: [/repo/lib/server_handler.py:73-76] (s.send_response(res); s.end_headers(); if out: s.wfile.write(atm_proto.encode(out, ...))). This shows failures return (500, None) in many code paths and so produce no body while successes return a dictionary and produce a body: see e.g. get_balance success vs failure [/repo/lib/server_handler.py:133-146] (mode_get_balance returns (200, {"account":..., "balance":...}) on success and (500, None) on failure).
- The encoding/encryption is deterministic and length-preserving up to block padding: [/repo/lib/atm_proto.py:27-31] (encode uses json.dumps to produce plaintext, then pads deterministically to the AES BLOCK_SIZE and encrypts with a fixed IV). Because padding is deterministic and no random padding is added, ciphertext length directly reflects plaintext length rounded up to the block size.
- Account balance formatting that affects plaintext length: [/repo/lib/account.py:21-26] (get_balance returns float("%0.2f" % self._balance) — balance is rendered with digits that affect message length). Account name length also directly appears in the JSON returned.
- Numerous success handlers include payloads containing account name and/or balance (mode_new_account, mode_get_balance, mode_deposit, mode_withdraw) while failure paths return None: see examples [/repo/lib/server_handler.py:117-129] (mode_new_account returns body on success), [/repo/lib/server_handler.py:151-164] (mode_deposit), [/repo/lib/server_handler.py:171-184] (mode_withdraw).
- The server never sets a Content-Length header for responses (the code calls s.send_response(res) and s.end_headers() but does not add Content-Length), so an observer can infer body length from the TCP stream or connection close behavior: [/repo/lib/server_handler.py:73-76].
Conclusion: Because success responses carry an encrypted but length-dependent body while failures do not, and because encryption adds no random-length padding, an attacker observing message lengths or connection metadata can distinguish outcomes and thereby infer account name/ balance information. This meets the repository's failure condition (Predictable fail/success response length and unprotected connection metadata).

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The bank server enforces that privileged actions (account creation, balance read, deposit, withdraw) are only executed after the incoming request is successfully decoded with the server's symmetric key and the one-time token in the decrypted payload matches the X-ATM-Token header. For account-sensitive operations (get_balance / deposit / withdraw) the server also verifies the PIN before making state changes. Requests that fail decoding, have a missing/mismatched token, or have a wrong/missing PIN result in a 500 response and no privileged state changes.

EVIDENCE:
- Server only processes requests after decoding and validating the token: [repo/lib/server_handler.py:59-67] (decode, validate_token, then call process) and [repo/lib/server_handler.py:73-76] (response written only after these steps).
- Token validation enforces non-empty token and exact match with the X-ATM-Token header (mismatch returns False): [repo/lib/server_handler.py:82-90]. The server only proceeds when validate_token(...) returns True: [repo/lib/server_handler.py:61-67].
- Account-sensitive operations require the PIN to match via account.check_pin(...) before any state changes; a PIN mismatch leads to a 500 and no mutation: get_balance [repo/lib/server_handler.py:133-146], deposit [repo/lib/server_handler.py:151-166], withdraw [repo/lib/server_handler.py:171-186].
- The ATM client constructs the encrypted payload and inserts the one-time token into both the encrypted payload and the X-ATM-Token header before sending: [repo/atm.py:20-24] (generate_token and add to params), [repo/atm.py:27-31] (X-ATM-Token header), and [repo/atm.py:33-36] (POST request sending encrypted data).

NOTES / LIMITATIONS:
- I attempted a dynamic run but the repository scripts target Python 2 (use of BaseHTTPServer, SocketServer, httplib) while python2 is not available in the execution environment; therefore I did not perform a runtime execution. However, the static code paths above provide direct, verifiable evidence that unauthenticated or malformed requests should not trigger privileged effects in this implementation (decoding/key and token checks gate processing; PIN checks gate per-account operations).
- Replay protection is weak (validate_token logs reused tokens but does not reject them), but playback/replay is explicitly out-of-scope for this test.

Files & lines referenced (for independent verification):
- repo/lib/server_handler.py:59-76, 82-95, 133-146, 151-166, 171-186
- repo/atm.py:20-24, 27-36

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The server and client code include defensive exception handling around all attacker-influenced I/O and protocol parsing paths so malformed/oversized inputs will not raise uncaught exceptions that break protocol integrity. Incoming HTTP POST bodies and decoded messages are processed inside try/except blocks and the server defaults to a safe 500 response when decoding/processing fails. Account operations also wrap logic in try/except and return error responses instead of letting exceptions escape.
EVIDENCE: 
- HTTP request parsing and POST body handling: /lib/server_handler.py:51-76 shows parsing of Content-Length and reading the body inside a try/except; decoding/processing of the request is inside a separate try/except with a default (res, out) = (500, None) so errors result in a 500 response rather than an uncaught exception. [/lib/server_handler.py:51-76]
- Default response and write-back behavior: /lib/server_handler.py:59-76 sets (res,out) default and in all failure cases sends response code res and only writes an encoded body when out is present, preventing partial state corruption. [/lib/server_handler.py:59-76]
- Detailed per-mode exception handling: each bank operation wraps its logic and catches exceptions, returning (500, None) on error: mode_new_account [/lib/server_handler.py:118-131], mode_get_balance [/lib/server_handler.py:134-149], mode_deposit [/lib/server_handler.py:151-169], mode_withdraw [/lib/server_handler.py:171-189]. These show server-side logic does not propagate exceptions to the server main loop.
- Top-level request-line length check prevents very large request-line attacks: /lib/server_handler.py:30-36 enforces a 65536 byte limit on the request line and returns 414 when exceeded. [/lib/server_handler.py:30-36]
- ATM client handles network/decode errors: /atm.py calls query_server inside try/except for client operations (e.g. mode_get_balance) so client-side decode/network exceptions cause a controlled exit via halt() instead of undefined behavior. Example: /atm.py:51-59 and query_server uses try/except around socket operations [/atm.py:19-49, 51-59].

Notes: While the code protects against uncaught exceptions that would break protocol integrity (hence PASS), it does not enforce an upper bound on Content-Length; extremely large Content-Length values could cause resource exhaustion (DoS) even if exceptions are caught. That is out-of-scope for the current test which focuses on uncaught exceptions and disrupted protocol state.
