tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: All ATM→BANK and BANK→ATM runtime messages that carry sensitive fields are fully encrypted with the shared symmetric key (authFile). The ATM constructs the full payload (username + token + card/token + operation/balance) and then calls authFile.encryptMessage before writing bytes to the socket; the Bank decrypts incoming packets with authFile.decryptMessage. The Bank builds responses (token and token+balance) and encrypts them with the same authFile before sending; the ATM decrypts them with authFile.decryptMessage. Although cardFile.encryptMessage is unimplemented (returns plaintext), it is always wrapped by the outer authFile symmetric encryption before network transmission, so no sensitive field is sent on the wire in plaintext.
EVIDENCE:

REASON: The symmetric encryption used for ATM<->BANK messages invokes Cipher.getInstance("AES") and initializes the Cipher with only the SecretKey (c.init(..., AESkey)) with no IV or per-message nonce. This uses the provider default (ECB) or otherwise no per-message IV, so there is no per-message fresh IV/seed — equivalent to a fixed/absent IV and failing the requirement for per-message freshness.
EVIDENCE: 
- ATM symmetric encrypt/decrypt (no IV used): [/workdir/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/authFile.java:62-73] shows c = Cipher.getInstance("AES"); c.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE,  AESkey); (no IV/nonce supplied).
- ATM symmetric decrypt (no IV used): [/workdir/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/authFile.java:77-92] shows c = Cipher.getInstance("AES"); c.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, k); (no IV/nonce supplied).
- BANK symmetric encrypt/decrypt (no IV used): [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/authFile.java:61-71] and [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/authFile.java:78-87] show identical usage: Cipher.getInstance("AES") followed by c.init(..., k) with no IV.
- No generation of per-message IV/nonce: there are no occurrences of IvParameterSpec or similar APIs in the repo; the symmetric cipher is initialized without any IV parameter. (See files above.)
- Additional context: ATM.cardFile.encryptMessage is unimplemented and returns plaintext [/workdir/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/cardFile.java:46-50], so per-message freshness is not introduced elsewhere.

Because the encryption path for ATM<->BANK messages uses AES without supplying a per-message IV/nonce (i.e., effectively ECB/no-IV), the test criterion requiring a non-fixed, per-message IV/seed is not met; therefore the repository FAILS the test.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository implements an explicit per-request freshness value (a 26-char token/nonces) generated with SecureRandom, includes it in requests and responses, and enforces freshness on acceptance paths: the Bank extracts and records (stores) tokens per account and rejects reuse, and the ATM checks that responses contain the same token it sent. The token size is bounded (substr(0,26) used) and tokens are tracked in account state to prevent replay.

EVIDENCE:
- Token generation (SecureRandom + BigInteger): [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/atm.java:55-57]
  - Shows creation of token: "SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom(); String token=new BigInteger(130, random).toString(32);"

- Token included in outgoing request messages (new-account and existing-account paths): [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/message.java:47-50] and [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/message.java:63]
  - New-account path prepends token twice: "mensaje=token+token+mensaje;" [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/message.java:47-50]
  - Existing-account path prepends token and card-file content: "mensaje=token+stringCFile+mensaje;" [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/message.java:63]

- Server extracts and bounds the token when parsing incoming requests: [/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/inputMessageChecker.java:20-24]
  - Token extraction uses substring(0,26): "String token= messageDecrypted2.substring(0, 26);" which enforces a fixed length parse.

- Server-side tracking and replay prevention (token recorded and checked): [/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/cuentas.java:36-41] and [/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/cuentas.java:66-75]
  - deposit/withdraw/getCurrentBalance check for prior use: "if (cu.tokens.contains(token)) throw new Exception (\"Token already used\"); cu.tokens.add(token);" [/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/cuentas.java:38-41, 72-75]
  - Account creation stores the initial token in the account state: [/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/cuenta.java:15-21] (constructor adds token to tokens list)

- Server echoes token in responses and ATM verifies it on receipt:
  - Server constructs responses containing the token: [/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:136-147] and [/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:152-156]
    - e.g. response = new messageResponse(messageData[1] + balance.toPlainString()); (token + data)
  - ATM checks the response begins with the token it sent: [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/atm.java:170-174]
    - "if (responseDecrypted.substring(0,26).compareTo(mensaje.getToken())!=0 ) { ... System.exit(255); }"

Notes / scope: 
- No timestamps are used (the protocol uses per-request nonces/tokens instead). That is acceptable for freshness if nonces are unique and tracked; here tokens are generated with SecureRandom and tracked per-account.
- Response-side token verification is performed by the ATM (the response receiver). The response-message class (responseMessage.decryptMessage) does not itself perform the comparison, but the ATM program does the check immediately after decrypting the response (evidence cited above).

Based on the concrete code evidence above, the repository provides explicit nonces, bounds them (fixed parsing length), records them per-account, prevents reuse by rejecting repeated tokens, and verifies freshness in responses. Therefore the test passes.

metadata.test_description: For every reachable security-relevant request/response exchange, the protocol uses an explicit freshness value (nonce/timestamp) when required, and receivers enforce freshness on all acceptance paths by validating it on receipt (including return/error paths), bounding it (no overflow / overly-large windows), and tracking it to prevent reuse; additionally, any freshness carried in responses that is relied upon by the protocol is also checked. Fails iff: `No nonce used`, `Nonce not checked on receive`, `Nonces not checked`, `Nonces not recorded`, `Response value nonce not checked`, `Nonce overflows`, `Timestamp window too large for nonce`, `Ignore check failure`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The ATM<->BANK messages are only encrypted with a shared symmetric cipher (AES); no keyed message-authentication code (MAC) is produced or verified. The code’s intended per-user signing (cardFile) is unimplemented, responses are encrypted-only, and parsing/acceptance is done after decryption without any separate MAC check. Therefore the repository fails the test (No MAC / Unkeyed encryption used; no MAC-on-return or MAC verification on error paths).

EVIDENCE:
- No MAC / unimplemented per-user signing: cardFile.encryptMessage is a stub that returns plaintext (no signature/MAC). See [repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/cardFile.java:46-56] which contains the comment and the implementation returning the raw bytes.
- Symmetric encryption used (no MAC): ATM-side authFile.encryptMessage / decryptMessage use Cipher.getInstance("AES") for encryption/decryption (no MAC). See [repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/authFile.java:62-73] and [repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/authFile.java:77-92]. The BANK-side symmetric functions likewise use AES-only: [repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/authFile.java:78-88] and decrypt [repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/authFile.java:61-71].
- Message construction uses the (unimplemented) per-user encrypt/sign and then wraps with auth-file AES encryption — still no MAC: see ATM message generation where cFile.encryptMessage is called and then aFile.encryptMessage wraps the whole payload: [repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/message.java:63-76]. Because cardFile.encryptMessage is a no-op, the only protection is the symmetric AES encryption from authFile.
- BANK does not verify any MAC / signature on the per-user portion; it simply decrypts with the auth key and parses token/cFile/message without verifying a signature or MAC: [repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/inputMessageChecker.java:10-24]. The file even comments an intended private-key decryption step that is not implemented.
- Responses are encrypted-only (no MAC): BANK’s messageResponse.encryptMessage returns authFile.encryptMessage(response) — AES-only — see [repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/messageResponse.java:1-13]. ATM decrypts the response and only checks that the first 26 bytes match the token, but this is done after AES decryption (no MAC/ tag verification): [repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/responseMessage.java:34-39] and the token comparison in atm main: [repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/atm.java:169-175].
- Error responses / paths: the server often prints "protocol_error" to its stdout in exception handlers and returns without sending a MAC- protected message to the client; multiple catch blocks in ClientServiceThread print a plain protocol_error and return, e.g. [repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:86-96] and catch blocks later where they print "protocol_error" and return (see [repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:30-56] and [repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:98-116]). This shows error paths are not delivering a separately MACed/authenticated error response that the ATM would verify.

Taken together these artifacts show: (1) there is no keyed MAC computed/checked anywhere; (2) the only protection is symmetric AES encryption (not a MAC); (3) the per-user signing step is unimplemented; (4) error/return paths are not covered by a MAC verification requirement. These directly violate the test’s requirements.

If you want, I can produce a small patch or instrumentation (e.g., add an HMAC over the plaintext and verify on all paths) and run a quick proof-of-fix demonstration. (That would require building/running the Java code.)

REASON: The bank produces responses whose plaintext lengths vary with operation and account balance (e.g. token-only vs token+balance), and those plaintexts are encrypted with a symmetric cipher whose ciphertext length depends on plaintext length. An observer can therefore distinguish/measure response lengths to infer whether an operation succeeded/failed or deduce balance magnitude.
EVIDENCE: 
- Bank sends different plaintext responses for different operations:
  - New-account ("n") path returns token only: [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:136-140]
  - Get-balance ("g") path returns token plus the balance string: [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:144-148]
  - Deposit/withdraw include token + amount similarly: [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:152-156] and [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:161-165]
- The response string is converted to bytes and encrypted via authFile.encryptMessage, so ciphertext length depends on plaintext length: [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/messageResponse.java:14-16] and [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/authFile.java:78-87] (c.doFinal on AES yields ciphertext whose length varies with plaintext length rounded to block size).
- ATM code pads the username to a fixed 250 bytes when constructing requests (mitigates username-length leakage), showing the authors attempted length-hiding for usernames, but no analogous padding is applied to responses including balances: [/workdir/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/message.java:22-26] and [/workdir/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/message.java:69-76].

Taken together: because responses include variable-length balance strings and are encrypted with a block cipher without any explicit length-hiding (constant-size responses or additional padding), an on-path observer can measure response lengths to distinguish operations and infer balances. This meets the FAIL condition (predictable fail/success response length / unprotected connection metadata).

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The BANK executes privileged actions (account creation and account operations) based on client-supplied fields without cryptographically verifying client credentials. The code path shows no enforcement of per-client credential verification (card-file signing) before performing privileged effects; the ATM-side card-file signing is unimplemented and BANK accepts the provided card/token values directly when creating accounts or processing requests. This allows an unauthenticated client (one that doesn't present/possess/verifiably prove credentials) to trigger privileged effects as long as they can send the symmetrically-encrypted message (auth-file usage aside).
EVIDENCE:
- Account creation uses client-supplied card/token without verification: [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:62-69] — in the "n" case the server calls createAccount(messageData[0], balance, messageData[2], messageData[1]) with values extracted from the request (no credential checks).
- The account record simply stores the provided cardFile and token and does not verify ownership: [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/cuentas.java:18-24] (createAccount implementation).
- The ATM-side card-file crypto is not implemented (no signature/encryption of per-client credentials): [/workdir/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/cardFile.java:46-56] (encryptMessage/decryptMessage are stubs returning plaintext).
- The ATM message construction for account creation embeds token twice and does not use a card-file signature for "n": [/workdir/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/message.java:47-51] (message for "n" uses mensaje=token+token+mensaje and messageEncrypted = mensaje.getBytes(...)). For non-"n" messages the code would call cFile.encryptMessage(...) but that method is a no-op (previous file), so no cryptographic client credential proof is enforced: [/workdir/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/message.java:63-66].
- The inputMessageChecker simply decrypts the symmetric envelope and slices out token/cardFile fields without performing a cryptographic verification of the cardFile ownership or a signature: [/workdir/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/inputMessageChecker.java:9-24].

Taken together, these code excerpts show that privileged operations can be triggered using client-supplied credential fields that are neither bound to the client by signatures nor otherwise verified; therefore an unauthenticated client can cause privileged effects and the test fails.

Notes: If you want a runtime demonstration, I can attempt to compile and run the ATM/BANK programs and show an example request (but the static code evidence above is sufficient to conclude FAIL).

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository generates card secrets (the contents of .card files) using Java SecureRandom to create a 130-bit random BigInteger (toString(32)) and writes that token as the card file contents. Card files are not derived by hashing the account name or any other public identifier; the default card filename may be account+".card" but the file contents are the random token. Bank code expects and checks the card-file string equality (not a deterministic derivation), so an attacker cannot compute the card secret from the public account identifier. This satisfies the test that card secrets are high-entropy and not deterministically derived.
EVIDENCE:
- Token generation (130-bit SecureRandom): [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/atm.java:55-57] shows SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom(); String token = new BigInteger(130, random).toString(32);
- Card file is written with that token when creating an account: [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/atm.java:188-193] (writer.write(token)).
- Message assembly for new-account (‘n’) places token twice and sends it as the card content: [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/message.java:47-50]. This demonstrates the token is the secret stored in the card file.
- cardFile object stores/reads raw token bytes (constructor used with token): [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/cardFile.java:31-36] (ficheroCard = token.getBytes()). Existing card files are read as raw bytes rather than being computed from the account: [/repo/ATMs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/atm/cardFile.java:19-25].
- On the BANK side the token and card-file string are extracted from the message and stored/checked as raw values (not derived from account): [/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/inputMessageChecker.java:20-24] and [/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/ClientServiceThread.java:62-69] (createAccount called with messageData[2] = cardFile and messageData[1] = token), and [/repo/BANKs/src/com/losquijotes/cybersecurity/bank/cuentas.java:38,72] shows the bank enforces equality of the provided card-file string against the stored value.

These code excerpts provide direct, verifiable evidence that card secrets are random tokens generated with SecureRandom (≈130 bits of entropy) and are not deterministic hashes of public identifiers. Therefore the test passes.

metadata.test_description: There is no exploitable vulnerability due to guessable/derivable card secrets: any card value used to authorize balance reads/writes is high-entropy and not deterministically derived from public identifiers. This fails if a MITM can guess/compute card secret due to lack of card randomness. Fails iff: `No randomness in card file`, `Card is hash of account name`.

REASON: Both the ATM and bank only send encrypted payloads over the network. The ATM places all sensitive fields (timestamp, account, pin, mode, amount) into a JSON array, pads and encrypts it with AES-CBC, computes an HMAC over the ciphertext, and sends only the HMAC + ciphertext. The bank similarly builds plaintext responses that include sensitive fields (account, balance, deposit, withdraw), but before sending it pads and encrypts with AES-CBC, computes an HMAC over the ciphertext, and sends only the HMAC + ciphertext. There are no other network send calls that transmit plaintext sensitive fields.

- ATM constructs the sensitive message (timestamp, account, pin, mode, amount): [/repo/atm.py:221-224]
- ATM pads and encrypts the message with AES-CBC, computes HMAC over the ciphertext, and composes the payload: [/repo/atm.py:225-237]
- ATM sends only the payload (HMAC + IV + ciphertext) over the network: [/repo/atm.py:240-251]
- Bank builds plaintext responses that include sensitive fields (account, initial_balance, deposit, withdraw, balance): [/repo/bank.py:132-159] and prints it to stdout: [/repo/bank.py:161-162]

- A repository-wide check for other send usages shows only these send calls (repo/atm.py and repo/bank.py). (See code locations above.)

Notes: The HMAC is sent in hex as a 64-character ASCII prefix, but it is a MAC over the ciphertext (not plaintext) using the shared secret key, so no plaintext sensitive bytes or individual sensitive fields are left outside the ciphertext.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The protocol uses timestamps for freshness, and the server enforces a 10s past-window and per-account monotonicity, but it does not bound future timestamps. An attacker can send a message with a far-future timestamp (ts >> now), which will pass the server's now - ts > 10 check (it is negative) and be accepted; the server then stores that future ts as the account's last timestamp, causing all subsequently legitimate (current-time) requests to be rejected (ts not > stored ts). Thus the implementation fails to enforce a bounded freshness window (no upper bound on timestamp/future-dated nonces), which violates the test criteria.
EVIDENCE:
- Client includes a timestamp in each request: [/workdir/repo/atm.py:222-224] (ts = time.time(); data = json.dumps([ts, account, pin, mode, amount]))
- Server parses and checks timestamps only for staleness (past window): [/workdir/repo/bank.py:120-131] (data = json.loads(plaintext); ts = data[0]; now = time.time(); if now - ts > 10: result = 'protocol_error')
- Server records timestamps per-account and enforces monotonicity for non-creation operations: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:132-136] (CREATE stores db[account] = (amount, ts)) and [/workdir/repo/bank.py:137-146] (for other ops the code requires db.has_key(account) and ts > db[account][1], then updates db[account] = (..., ts) on success). See also updates on withdraw/check: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:149-159].
- Missing upper-bound check: there is no code that rejects timestamps that are too far in the future (e.g. comparing ts > now + delta); the only freshness bound is a one-sided past check (now - ts > 10). This allows acceptance of arbitrarily-future timestamps which can then be recorded and prevent future valid requests.

Because of the missing upper bound on timestamps (allowing future-dated timestamps to be accepted and recorded), the repository fails the test case.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The server constructs plaintext responses whose lengths vary with success/failure and with account name/balance, then pads only to the AES block size and sends a hex HMAC tag plus the ciphertext. An observer of the total response length (or the ciphertext length) can distinguish error vs success and infer account-specific information (account name or balance). This violates the requirement that metadata (message length) not leak account name or balance.

EVIDENCE:
1) Bank constructs variable-length JSON responses on success vs failure:
   - Initial/default and protocol error values: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:82-96] (result = '{}', protocol_error assignment)
   - CREATE success response: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:132-136] (result = '{"account":"%s","initial_balance":%.2f}')
   - DEPOSIT success response: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:144-148] (result = '{"account":"%s","deposit":%.2f}')
   - WITHDRAW success response: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:150-154] (result = '{"account":"%s","withdraw":%.2f}')
   - CHECK balance response: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:156-160] (result = '{"account":"%s","balance":%.2f}')

2) Bank only pads to AES block size and sends tag + ciphertext (so total message length depends on result length): [/workdir/repo/bank.py:165-179]
   - Padding to 16 bytes: line showing l = 16 - (len(result) % 16) and result += chr(l) * l
   - Encrypt: iv + cipher.encrypt(result)
   - Hash and send: payload = h.hexdigest() + c; conn.send(payload)

3) Client parses tag as the first 64 bytes and ciphertext afterwards, confirming the tag is hex text concatenated with raw ciphertext: [/workdir/repo/atm.py:258-266, 276-283]
   - atm.py reads response and slices tag = response[:64]; ciphertext = response[64:]
   - This shows the wire format is ascii hex tag (64 bytes) followed by ciphertext, so an observer can measure payload length.

4) Reproducible runtime evidence showing different total payload lengths for different plaintext results (saved artifact): /evidence/artifacts/payload_lengths.txt
   - Example lines (excerpt):
     {'result': '{}', 'len_payload': 96}
     {'result': 'protocol_error', 'len_payload': 96}
     {'result': '{"account":"alice","balance":100.00}', 'len_payload': 128}
     {'result': '{"account":"averylongaccountname_exceedingxxxxxxxxxx","balance":12345.67}', 'len_payload': 160}
   - Full contents: [/evidence/artifacts/payload_lengths.txt]
   - These were generated by replicating the bank's padding/encryption/HMAC composition and show clear, measurable length differences between error vs success and between different account names/balances.

Conclusion: Because the total response size (tag + ciphertext) varies predictably with the plaintext result (which includes account name and balance), an on-path observer can distinguish success vs failure and infer account-related information from message length metadata. Therefore the test FAILs.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The server implementation (bank.py) contains multiple reachable, attacker-influenced code paths where malformed or unexpected input can raise uncaught exceptions (e.g. JSON parsing errors, indexing errors, other socket errors). The code only partially validates inputs and only catches socket.timeout in critical places, so exceptions like ValueError/IndexError/other socket errors can propagate and crash or disrupt protocol state.
EVIDENCE: 
- Lack of general exception handling around receive and parsing: the accept/recv block only catches socket.timeout, allowing other exceptions to propagate (repo/bank.py:87-96).
  - [repo/bank.py:87-96] shows try: (conn, addr) = s.accept(); msg = conn.recv(1024) followed by except socket.timeout: — other exceptions are uncaught.
- Unsafe decryption / padding handling: padded[-1] and slicing are used without guarding against empty or malformed ciphertext which can raise IndexError or produce incorrect ord() usage (repo/bank.py:108-111).
  - [repo/bank.py:108-111] cipher.decrypt(ciphertext)[16:]; pbytes = ord(padded[-1]); plaintext = padded[:-pbytes]
- Unprotected JSON parsing and index assumptions: the plaintext is passed directly into json.loads and then indexed into without try/except or length/type checks; a malformed plaintext will raise ValueError or IndexError and crash the server (repo/bank.py:120-126).
  - [repo/bank.py:120-126] data = json.loads(plaintext); ts = data[0]; account = data[1]; pin = data[2]; mode = data[3]; amount = data[4]
- Client-side code also lacks broad exception handling for send/recv and parsing of the server response; only socket.timeout is caught, so unexpected conditions can raise uncaught exceptions on the client (repo/atm.py:249-255, 258-274).
  - [repo/atm.py:249-255] try: s.send(payload); response = s.recv(1024) except socket.timeout: — other socket errors will propagate.
  - [repo/atm.py:261-274] response parsing uses slicing and padding removal without guarding against malformed response contents (tag = response[:64]; ciphertext = response[64:]; iv = ciphertext[:16]; check len(iv) but then decrypt and pbytes=ord(padded[-1]) with no exception handling).

These lines are direct evidence in the source that attacker-controlled input can lead to uncaught exceptions (ValueError from json.loads, IndexError from padded[-1], socket-related exceptions) which can disrupt protocol integrity. Because the code does not guard these operations with appropriate try/except or validation, the test fails.

REASON: All atm<->bank runtime messages carrying sensitive fields (account, card file, operation, amounts/balance) are transmitted inside an encrypted payload: encsock_help.socket_send AES-encrypts the entire application payload (bin_data) and appends an HMAC; the receiver uses socket_recv which verifies the HMAC then AES-decrypts the enc_data. Amounts receive additional inline encryption before being embedded, but that inline ciphertext is then included in the overall encrypted payload as well. No code path sends account/operation/balance fields as plaintext on the wire.
EVIDENCE: 
- Message construction on the ATM side: atm constructs the payload as a delimiter-separated string including account, card file, operation and amount, then calls encsock_help.socket_send to transmit it [/repo/atmsrc/atm.py:136-141, 151-155, 165-169, 179-183, 213-220].
- Core send implementation (encryption of full payload + MAC): encsock_help.socket_send encrypts (AES-CTR) the entire bin_data and computes a MAC over nonce+enc_data, then sends header (length, nonce, timestamp, header_mac) followed by enc_data and mac_data [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:206-234, 221-223, 156-173].
- Inline amount encryption (also embedded and then the whole message encrypted): encrypt_inline produces nonce+ciphertext hex for amounts; socket_send substitutes this in the payload and then encrypts the whole payload as above [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:190-196, 206-216, 222].
- Bank-side receiving and responding: bank spawn_thread calls encsock_help.socket_recv to parse/verify/decrypt incoming messages and later uses encsock_help.socket_send to reply; thus both directions use the same encrypted wire format [/repo/banksrc/bank.py:185-191, 206-211].

These code excerpts show the network stream carries only the header (length, random nonce, timestamp, header_mac) and enc_data+mac_data; the sensitive plaintext fields are inside enc_data and are not sent plaintext. Therefore the test passes.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The code generates a fresh random nonce per encrypted message (via encsock_help.gen_rand) and uses that nonce as the per-message input to the encryption flow. There is no hardcoded or global constant IV/seed used across encryptions; each socket_send/encrypt_inline call generates a new 16-byte nonce.
EVIDENCE: 
- Random nonce generation: gen_rand uses Crypto.Random.new().read to produce rand_len bytes [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:39-44].
  - [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:39-44]
- Inline encryption creates a fresh nonce before encrypting amounts: encrypt_inline calls gen_rand(_nonce_len) and passes it to aes_encrypt [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:191-196].
  - [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:191-196]
- Per-message nonce in socket_send: socket_send generates nonce = gen_rand(_nonce_len) for each message and includes it in the header and in the call to aes_encrypt([repo/shared/encsock_help.py:206-223,231-235]).
  - [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:206-223]
  - [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:227-235]
- aes_encrypt/aes_decrypt take nonce as an argument and derive an ephemeral key by XORing the per-message nonce with the stored encryption_key (so the effective cipher key is different per message) before creating the AES-CTR object [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:136-146,156-173].
  - [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:136-146]
  - [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:156-173]
- The ATM reads its encryption key from an auth file at runtime (so the symmetric key is not a hardcoded constant) and then calls socket_send which generates the per-message nonce [repo/atm:358-362, 436-443].
  - [repo/atm:358-362]
  - [repo/atm:436-443]

Taken together, this shows every encryption path for ATM<->bank messages uses a freshly-generated nonce (IV seed) per-message rather than a fixed constant. Therefore the test PASSes.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository consistently uses explicit freshness values (a 16-byte nonce and a millisecond timestamp) in every networked request/response exchange, and both senders and receivers verify and enforce freshness: header MAC binds nonce+timestamp, socket_recv verifies header MAC and message MAC, each side checks the timestamp against a 15-second window, records nonces and timestamps to prevent reuse, and treats freshness-check failures as protocol errors. There is no evidence of acceptance paths that skip nonce/timestamp validation or of unbounded windows/overflow in the timestamp handling.

EVIDENCE:
- Nonce + timestamp generation and inclusion in the protocol header (sender): [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:218-235] shows generation of a 16-byte nonce, creation of a timestamp (millisecond resolution), and assembly of the header and body sent over the socket.
- Header parsing and MAC validation (receiver): [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:83-96] and [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:116-126] show socket_recv reading the fixed-size header, extracting read_length/nonce/timestamp, verifying a header MAC computed over (length, nonce, timestamp), verifying the message MAC over (nonce, enc_data), and returning (nonce, timestamp, data).
- Inline encryption/decryption (payload-level nonce) is present but protected by the outer header MAC/encryption; inline nonces are generated/decrypted inside [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:190-205]. The protocol's freshness checks operate on the header nonce/timestamp, not on these inline nonces.
- Server-side freshness enforcement and replay protection: [/repo/banksrc/bank.py:185-205] (spawn_thread) shows the server calling encsock_help.socket_recv(), computing current_timestamp, purging old entries older than current_timestamp - 15*1000, rejecting messages whose nonce is already seen or whose timestamp is older than the window (raising a protocol error), and then recording the new (timestamp, nonce).
- Client-side (ATM) freshness enforcement and replay protection: [/repo/atmsrc/atm.py:217-236] shows the ATM recording the current timestamp just before transmission, calling socket_send/socket_recv, purging old stored nonces older than current_timestamp - 15*1000, rejecting responses when the nonce was already seen or when the response timestamp is older than expected, and then recording the nonce/timestamp.
- All replies (including error returns) are sent using encsock_help.socket_send (see [/repo/banksrc/bank.py:206-211]) so responses carry fresh header nonce/timestamp and will be validated by the receiver (see ATM receive checks above).

Notes / justification of correctness against fail conditions:
- "No nonce used": False — every message includes a generated nonce (encsock_help.socket_send).
- "Nonce not checked on receive": False — socket_recv returns nonce/timestamp only after MAC/header checks and both bank and ATM check nonce/timestamp before accepting/processing (banksrc spawn_thread and atmsrc send code cited above).
- "Nonces not recorded": False — both sides append nonce and timestamp to replay_check_nonce/replay_check_ts and purge entries older than 15s (banksrc & atmsrc cited above).
- "Response value nonce not checked": Responses use the same framing and are validated by the receiver (ATM checks replies); inline payload nonces exist for confidentiality but are protected by outer header MAC and are not used for freshness decisions.
- "Nonce overflows" / "Timestamp window too large for nonce": Timestamp is encoded in 6 bytes (encsock_help._timestamp_len = 6) and current ms-since-epoch fits comfortably in 6 bytes for the foreseeable future; window is explicitly bounded to 15 seconds in the code.
- "Ignore check failure": On check failures the code raises SystemExit/socket.error which is caught and triggers a protocol error / connection close (see [/repo/banksrc/bank.py:212-216] and [/repo/atmsrc/atm.py:259-261]).

Because the checks are implemented in the shared framing (encsock_help) and exercised on all server/client send/receive code paths, and because failures are handled as protocol errors, I conclude the repository PASSes the freshness / nonce requirements in the test case.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The code implements a keyed HMAC (HMAC-SHA256) and enforces MAC verification on all received messages (both header and payload) before any processing; outgoing (return/error) messages are sent using the same socket_send which computes and attaches MACs. Both ATM and bank sides set the shared key (bank writes auth file, ATM reads it) and use encsock_help.socket_recv/socket_send for all network I/O, so acceptance is conditioned on a keyed MAC and verification is enforced on all acceptance/return paths.

EVIDENCE:
- Keyed MAC implementation (HMAC-SHA256) and use of a shared key:
  - [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:69-79] easy_mac uses hmac.new(encsock_help.encryption_key, ..., hashlib.sha256)
  - [/repo/atmsrc/atm.py:95-99] ATM reads the auth file and sets encsock_help.encryption_key
  - [/repo/banksrc/bank.py:30-33] Bank creates the auth file and sets encsock_help.encryption_key

- MAC verification on incoming messages (header and payload) before accepting data:
  - [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:83-96] socket_recv reads header and verifies header_mac via easy_mac; raises socket.error if mismatch
  - [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:119-122] socket_recv verifies payload MAC (mac_data) via easy_mac; raises socket.error on mismatch

- Outgoing messages (including return/error responses) are MACed before sending:
  - [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:221-235] socket_send performs encrypt-then-mac, sets mac_data and header_mac, and sends the combined stream
  - [/repo/banksrc/bank.py:209-211] After receive(...) computes result, bank calls encsock_help.socket_send(socket_conn, result) to send reply (so replies are MACed)

- All network I/O paths use the encapsulating helpers that perform MAC checks:
  - [/repo/banksrc/bank.py:185-211] spawn_thread obtains (nonce, timestamp, data) = encsock_help.socket_recv(socket_conn) (so messages are checked before parsing) and calls socket_send for replies. Note the except block ([/repo/banksrc/bank.py:212-215]) prints protocol_error and closes the connection on socket error (i.e., MAC verification failures do not lead to accepting or replying with unchecked content).
  - [/repo/atmsrc/atm.py:213-221] send() uses encsock_help.socket_send to transmit and then encsock_help.socket_recv to receive and verify the bank reply before using it.

Given these artifacts, the repository meets the test: messages are MACed with a keyed HMAC, verification is enforced on receipt (both header and payload), and replies are also MACed; error paths caused by MAC failures result in connection termination and are not accepted. No evidence of unkeyed MACs or missing MAC checks on return/error paths was found.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The protocol reveals observable, predictable differences in message lengths between error (failure) and successful responses and message length also varies with the account name length (modulo AES block-size). This allows a network observer to infer whether an operation succeeded (and leakage about account name length), violating the property that an attacker cannot use metadata to derive an account's name or balance.
EVIDENCE: 
- The response encoding clearly builds a binary stream whose length depends on the encrypted payload length: the send path computes a length from the encrypted data and sends header+enc_data+mac. See socket_send where amount is inline-encrypted then the AES-encrypted payload length and header are composed: [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:208-236].
- The amount field is protected by inline encryption with a fixed zfill(1024), so the numerical balance itself does not change message size. However the rest of the message (account name, card data, mode string) is encrypted as part of the payload and its plaintext length affects the encrypted payload length: the amount encryption line and zero-padding are here: [repo/shared/encsock_help.py:210-215, 212-214].
- The bank returns short, fixed, human-readable error codes for failures (e.g. '1|||', '2|||', '23|||', '99|||') but includes the account name in successful responses (e.g. result = "0|account|balance|<amount>") — see receive where missing-argument errors are returned and where success messages include the account name: [repo/banksrc/bank.py:40-76] and [repo/banksrc/bank.py:142-151]. Because success responses include the account name and are incorporated into the encrypted payload, the total packet size differs between failure and success.
- The ATM constructs requests that include the account name and (base64) card file, which affect message length: [repo/atmsrc/atm.py:137-141]. The ATM also decodes the response by splitting on the delimiter and expecting the account name in the response: [repo/atmsrc/atm.py:240-249].
- Practical experiment (script run in this environment) that uses the repository encsock helper to construct/send two example responses into a dummy socket shows a large, predictable size difference between an error response and a successful response (and shows total message length changes when account name length changes). The exact measured outputs were saved to /evidence/artifacts/lengths.txt and include: 
  * error len= 104 header_read_len= 48 total_stream_len= 104
  * success len= 2232 header_read_len= 2176 total_stream_len= 2232
  * acct=a total_len=2216 header_read_len=2160
  * acct=bob total_len=2216 header_read_len=2160
  * acct=alice total_len=2232 header_read_len=2176
  * acct=longusername1234567890 total_len=2248 header_read_len=2192
  Evidence file: [/evidence/artifacts/lengths.txt]

These show that an observer can distinguish error vs success (different packet sizes) and can observe changes in total packet size correlated with account name length (leaking name-length information). Therefore the repository FAILs the test condition.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The server enforces authenticated channels via HMAC checks before processing requests (encsock_help verifies header and payload MACs) and catches socket errors raised on authentication failure, printing "protocol_error" and not calling the request handler. An unauthenticated raw TCP client triggered a protocol error and did not cause account creation; a properly-authenticated ATM client (using bank.auth) successfully executed a privileged action (account creation). Thus unauthenticated clients cannot trigger privileged effects.
EVIDENCE: 
- Authentication checks in the transport layer: [/workdir/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:83-96] verifies header MAC and [/workdir/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:119-122] verifies payload MAC; these lines cause socket.error if MACs do not match.
- Server handling of socket-level errors without performing privileged actions: [/workdir/repo/banksrc/bank.py:185-215] shows spawn_thread calling encsock_help.socket_recv(...) then in the except (socket.timeout, socket.error, SystemExit) branch it prints "protocol_error" and closes the connection without calling receive/performing actions.
- Server request validation requires account and card presence: [/workdir/repo/banksrc/bank.py:40-50] (returns an error '2|||' if card field missing), and create-account logic at [/workdir/repo/banksrc/bank.py:52-71] which only proceeds after these checks.
- Runtime experiment (logs saved under /evidence/artifacts): the bank server was started; an unauthenticated raw TCP client sent arbitrary bytes and the server logged "protocol_error" instead of performing an action; then the authenticated ATM client created an account successfully.
  - Artifact: /evidence/artifacts/bank.log (contains the server output showing "created", "protocol_error", and the ATM response)
  - Artifact: /evidence/artifacts/experiment.txt (transcript of commands and outputs used during testing)

Repro steps (what I ran, reproduced in the artifacts):
1) Built & started the server: (in repo) python3 bank &> /tmp/bank.log &
2) Sent unauthenticated raw TCP bytes: python3 -c "import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.connect(('127.0.0.1',3000)); s.sendall(b'HELLO'); s.close()"
   Result observed in /evidence/artifacts/bank.log: protocol_error
3) Ran the client ATM to create an account (authenticated via bank.auth): ./atm -a alice -n 10.00
   Result: {"account":"alice","initial_balance":10.00} (also appears in /evidence/artifacts/bank.log)

Because the server fails closed on unauthenticated inputs (socket_recv raises socket.error which is caught and leads to no privileged effects), the test requirement is satisfied: unauthenticated clients cannot trigger privileged actions.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The ATM client contains an unchecked unpack of the server response which can raise a ValueError when a malicious/modified server message lacks the expected 4 '|' separated fields. That ValueError is not handled inside the send() method and will propagate up, causing the ATM process to exit (observed exit code 255). This is an uncaught exception reachable via attacker-influenced server->client data (a MITM can modify the server reply), so the implementation fails the test.
EVIDENCE: 
- Runtime reproduction demonstrating the exception: /evidence/artifacts/test_atm_uncaught.py (created test) and its output /evidence/artifacts/test_out.txt showing the ValueError: "not enough values to unpack (expected 4, got 1)". (See contents below.)
  - /evidence/artifacts/test_out.txt (excerpt):
    CAUGHT EXCEPTION IN TEST: ValueError not enough values to unpack (expected 4, got 1)
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "/evidence/artifacts/test_atm_uncaught.py", line 28, in <module>
        a.send('irrelevant')
      File "/evidence/artifacts/test_atm_uncaught.py", line 19, in send
        error, acct_name, mode, val = data.split(self._delimiter)
      File "/evidence/artifacts/test_atm_uncaught.py", line 19, in send
        error, acct_name, mode, val = data.split(self._delimiter)
    ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 4, got 1)

- Source showing the vulnerable unpack and the exception handling (or lack thereof):
  - /workdir/repo/atm: send() does the unpack without checking the number of parts [ /workdir/repo/atm:436-466 ]. Specifically: "error, acct_name, mode, val = data.split(self._delimiter)" [/workdir/repo/atm:456-458].
  - The send() method only catches socket.timeout, socket.error, ConnectionRefusedError, ConnectionResetError, and SystemExit; it does not catch ValueError that would be raised by the failed unpack (see except clauses) [/workworkdir/repo/atm:466-475].
  - The top-level invocation wraps application().run() in a broad except Exception which converts any unhandled exception into an exit(255) (so the client process exits) [/workdir/repo/atm:478-481].

- Protocol-level handling on the server side shows the bank prints "protocol_error" for malformed input and remains running (i.e., the server is robust), but the client is not: example bank output showing the server handling malformed messages without crashing: /tmp/bank_out.txt (created during dynamic testing) contains repeated "protocol_error" lines (excerpt):
  created
  protocol_error
  protocol_error

Why this fails the test: An attacker (e.g. MITM) can modify the server->client reply so that it does not contain the expected '|' separated fields; when the ATM client receives such a message it performs an unchecked split/unpack which raises ValueError. That exception is not handled inside the send() path and results in the ATM process exiting (integrity of the protocol disrupted). This is a concrete, reproducible uncaught exception caused by attacker-influenced runtime interaction.

What would be needed to PASS: The ATM client must validate the number of fields returned by data.split(self._delimiter) (and generally validate message formats/lengths) and handle parse failures gracefully rather than allowing ValueError to cause process termination. 

Files produced as evidence (all saved under /evidence/artifacts/):
- /evidence/artifacts/test_atm_uncaught.py  (test harness that reproduces the unpacking ValueError)
- /evidence/artifacts/test_out.txt       (output + traceback from running the harness)

Cited source locations:
- /workdir/repo/atm:436-466 (send method) and 478-481 (top-level exception handler)
- /workdir/repo/bank:412-435 (server spawn_thread which shows server handles malformed messages and prints "protocol_error")

Because the client can be forced to crash by attacker-controlled server responses, this repository FAILs the test.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The ATM creates per-account card values from cryptographically-random bytes (encsock_help.gen_rand) and the bank treats the card value as an opaque string and checks equality; there is no code deriving the card from the account name (the only hash-based construction is commented out). Therefore the card secret is not deterministically derived from public identifiers and is generated with randomness.
EVIDENCE: 
- Card-file size constant showing length 10 bytes: [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:21-23] ("_cardfile_size = 10").
- Random generator implementation using Crypto.Random: [/repo/shared/encsock_help.py:38-43] (encsock_help.gen_rand reads rand_len bytes from Crypto.Random.new()).
- ATM generates the card using gen_rand and base64-encodes it before writing the .card file: [/repo/atmsrc/atm.py:101-112] (createCardFile uses encsock_help.gen_rand(encsock_help._cardfile_size) then base64.encodebytes(...)).
- Commented-out alternate (hash-based) card derivation is present but disabled, demonstrating the intended random approach: [/repo/atmsrc/atm.py:104-108] (these lines are commented out).
- Bank verifies the provided card by direct equality against the stored card value (no hash-of-account logic): [/repo/banksrc/bank.py:88-92] (acct_card_value != card_value check) and stores the card value when creating the account: [/repo/banksrc/bank.py:71-72] (self.acct_cards.append(card_value)).

These file excerpts are present in the repository and show the card is generated from random bytes (not derived from the account name) and used as an opaque secret for authorization.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: All ATM<->Bank network I/O is performed over OpenSSL TLS (SSL_write/SSL_read). The ATM crafts messages containing sensitive fields (account name, operation, dollar, cent) and passes that message buffer to the SSL client code which transmits it using SSL_write; the Bank server receives messages via SSL_read and responds with SSL_write. Thus sensitive payload bytes are sent inside the TLS-encrypted channel and there is no code path that writes those payload bytes via an unencrypted socket send API.

EVIDENCE:
- ATM composes the request (sensitive fields included) into a buffer: [/repo/atm.c:112-116] shows memcpy of Auth_id and snprintf of "#%s %c %ld %d#" (Accountname, Operation, Dollar, Cent).
- Client sends the message using TLS: [/repo/atmclient.c:151-156] (n = SSL_write(ssl, cmdstr,clen);) and uses SSL_read to receive the reply [/repo/atmclient.c:169-176]. The SSL context/connection setup (SSL_new, SSL_set_fd, SSL_connect) is at [/repo/atmclient.c:136-142].
- Server receives and sends via TLS: [/repo/bankserver.c:154-157] (n = SSL_read(ssl, buffer,PROTOCOLMSGLEN);) and [/repo/bankserver.c:184-186] (n = SSL_write(ssl, Msgstr,PROTOCOLMSGLEN);). The server initializes TLS and loads certificates at [/repo/bankserver.c:233-239] and [/repo/bankserver.c:109-129] (LoadCertificates uses SSL_CTX_use_certificate_file and SSL_CTX_use_PrivateKey_file).
- Build links OpenSSL (indicating intended TLS usage) in Makefile: [/repo/Makefile:4] and [/repo/Makefile:28] include -lssl -lcrypto.

Notes: There is no use of plain send()/write() or unencrypted socket sends for ATM<->Bank messages in the codebase (network I/O is via SSL_read/SSL_write). Local printing of messages to stdout (e.g., printf of Msgstr) does not affect on-the-wire encryption.

This evidence is static code inspection showing that all reachable network send/receive calls for ATM<->Bank use OpenSSL TLS.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: All atm<->bank messages are transported over OpenSSL TLS (SSL_write/SSL_read). There is no custom per-message encryption in the repository that hardcodes an IV or seeds a PRNG with a fixed constant. The only explicit use of OpenSSL randomness in the repo is RAND_bytes() in authfile.c to create an auth_id (which is per-file random), and there are no occurrences of RAND_seed/RAND_add/srand/rand or any EVP/AES/DES encryption APIs that would indicate manual IV handling.
EVIDENCE:
- Network messages use OpenSSL/TLS for encryption (no custom cipher/IV handling): [repo/atmclient.c:129-156] shows SSL_library_init(), SSL_connect(), and SSL_write. [repo/bankserver.c:149-186] shows SSL_accept(), SSL_read(), and SSL_write handling messages. [repo/bankserver.c:233-239] shows server TLS initialization and certificate loading.
- Randomness usage is limited to creating an auth file: [repo/authfile.c:44-48] calls RAND_bytes(auth_id, AUTH_IDBYTESIZE).
- Repository-wide search summary (stored artifact) showing absence of custom cipher/IV/seed usages and listing the grep checks performed: [/evidence/artifacts/search_results.txt]

Details so the check can be independently verified:
- The client sends messages via SSL_write and the server handles them via SSL_read/SSL_write; therefore IV/nonce selection for record-layer encryption is performed internally by the OpenSSL library rather than by application code. The repository contains no code that sets a fixed IV or seeds the RNG with a fixed constant for those encryptions.

If you would like, I can additionally:
- Run a grep and attach the full grep outputs as artifacts (already summarized), or
- Instrument the code to log any calls to OpenSSL RAND APIs at runtime.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The ATM<->bank protocol does not use a keyed message-authentication code (MAC). The ATM transmits the raw shared authentication value (Auth_id) as part of the message (i.e. the key itself is sent in the clear), and the bank only checks equality of those bytes rather than verifying a MAC over the message. Responses from the bank are not authenticated at all. This violates the test criteria (Unkeyed MAC and No MAC on return).
EVIDENCE: 
- ATM includes the authentication value (Auth_id) verbatim at the start of the message it sends to the bank: [/repo/atm.c:112-116] (memcpy(tobankstr,Auth_id,AUTH_IDBYTESIZE); then snprintf the rest).
- Bank extracts those bytes and compares them directly to its Auth_id byte-for-byte (no MAC verification, just equality): [/repo/bankcommand.c:32-41] (memcpy(auth_id,str1,AUTH_IDBYTESIZE); while (i<AUTH_IDBYTESIZE) { if (auth_id[i]!=Auth_id[i]) { ... }}).
- The bank generates a random authentication value and writes it to the auth file (this is a shared secret), which the ATM later reads; but the protocol sends that secret in the clear rather than using it to compute a MAC: [/repo/authfile.c:44-59] (RAND_bytes(auth_id, AUTH_IDBYTESIZE); fwrite(auth_id,...)).
- Bank responses are plain strings constructed by printoutput with no authentication tag appended: [/repo/check.c:13-20,33-39,56-61] (snprintf into Msgstr) and returned by handlerequest [/repo/bankcommand.c:105-126].
- The ATM client receives the bank response and accepts/prints it with no verification of any authentication tag: [/repo/atmclient.c:169-192] (SSL_read into buffer; then immediately compare to TRANSACTION_FAIL and copy to Msgstr / print).

Together these show: (1) No keyed MAC is computed or verified (the key is embedded in the message instead), (2) responses are unauthenticated, and (3) verification performed by the bank is an equality check of the sent secret rather than verification of a keyed MAC — matching the FAIL conditions (Unkeyed MAC and No MAC on return).

An on-path observer can therefore see the client->server packet lengths and infer account name/amount metadata. This violates the requirement that an MITM cannot derive an account's name or balance from observable metadata.
EVIDENCE: 
- Client crafts the request including account name and amounts: [/repo/atm.c:112-117] (memcpy of Auth_id and snprintf to build "#%s %c %ld %d#" including Accountname, Dollar, Cent).

- Server uses a fixed-size write for responses (so server->client response lengths are constant): [/repo/bankserver.c:184-186] (n = SSL_write(ssl, Msgstr, PROTOCOLMSGLEN);). The fixed response length alone does not prevent leakage from the client->server direction.
- PROTOCOLMSGLEN constant (message buffer length): [/repo/global.h:35-36] (PROTOCOLMSGLEN 340) — corroborates server fixed-size send.

Because the client-side requests are variable-length and include the account name/amount, an adversary observing connection metadata (message lengths) can infer account names or balances. Therefore the test fails.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The server enforces an in-message credential (Auth_id) but does not perform TLS/client-level authentication of the connecting peer. Privileged operations are gated only on the message-level auth_id check (which an unauthenticated client can send), so an unauthenticated client that supplies the correct credentials in its request can trigger privileged effects.
EVIDENCE: 
- The request contains and is checked against the server's Auth_id: [repo/bankcommand.c:32-43] (memcpy of AUTH_IDBYTESIZE from the start of the message and byte-by-byte compare to Auth_id) and [repo/bankcommand.c:89-97] (handlerequest returns PARSE_ERROR or STILLALIVE based on parse/credential check). These lines show the server accepts requests and allows the transaction only if the in-message auth_id matches the stored Auth_id.
- The server reads and serves over an SSL/TLS connection but never sets up client verification: SSL handshake and I/O occur (SSL_accept and SSL_read/SSL_write) in [repo/bankserver.c:149-156] and the accept loop that creates the SSL object in [repo/bankserver.c:258-260]. The TLS context and certificate loading are created in [repo/bankserver.c:86-99] and [repo/bankserver.c:109-129], but there is no code that requests or verifies client certificates (no calls such as SSL_CTX_set_verify or SSL_get_verify_result are present in the repo).
- The repository creates the Auth file and random auth_id bytes here: [repo/authfile.c:36-64] (create_authfile writes random AUTH_IDBYTESIZE bytes to the auth file). This shows the credential mechanism is message-based, not TLS client-auth based.
- Corroborating evidence that no client-verify calls exist in the repo: [/evidence/artifacts/grep_ssl_verify.txt] (empty output indicates functions used to enable/require client certificate verification are not present in the codebase).

Conclusion: Because the code does not perform channel-level (client) authentication and relies solely on an in-message Auth_id for authorizing privileged actions, an unauthenticated client (one that is not TLS-client-authenticated) that sends a valid auth_id can perform privileged actions — therefore the test fails.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository does not use card file contents as an authentication secret for balance reads/writes. The actual authentication token (Auth_id) is generated with OpenSSL RAND_bytes (high-entropy) and is the value verified by the bank. Card files are created empty and their filenames are deterministically derived from account names, but these card files are only used locally as existence/mapping checks on the ATM side and are not used to authorize requests to the bank.
EVIDENCE:
- Card files are created empty (no randomness written): create_cardfile simply opens and closes the file without writing any secret [repo/cardfile.c:74-89].
- Card filenames are derived from the account name (deterministic): createCardname concatenates Accountname + ".card" to form the card filename [repo/cardfile.c:94-103].
- Authentication token is generated with RAND_bytes (cryptographically-random bytes) and written to the auth file: create_authfile uses RAND_bytes(auth_id, AUTH_IDBYTESIZE) and writes AUTH_IDBYTESIZE bytes to the auth file [repo/authfile.c:36-65]; bytes size defined as 32 in global.h [repo/global.h:39-42].
- The ATM reads the auth file and prepends this Auth_id to messages sent to the bank (so Auth_id is used for network authentication), showing that auth is based on Auth_id, not card contents [repo/atm.c:95-116].
- The bank extracts the auth token from the incoming message and performs a byte-by-byte comparison against its Auth_id to authenticate the client [repo/bankcommand.c:32-43].

Conclusion: Although card filenames are deterministic and card files contain no randomness, they are not used as the secret for authorizing balance operations. The authoritative authentication secret is Auth_id, which is high-entropy and created with RAND_bytes. Therefore the test condition (no exploitable vulnerability due to guessable/derivable card secrets) PASSES for this repository.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The AES encryption in both the ATM and bank code generates a fresh per-encryption IV using Crypto.Random on every call to encrypt (iv = Random.new().read(AES.block_size)). There is no hardcoded or global constant IV or explicit fixed RNG seed used for IV generation in the reachable encryption code paths.

EVIDENCE:
- AESCipher.encrypt in atm creates a fresh IV per call: [repo/atm.py:45-49]
  - /workdir/repo/atm.py lines 45-49:
    45	def encrypt(self, raw):
    46	    raw = self._pad(raw)
    47	    iv = Random.new().read(AES.block_size)
    48	    cipher = AES.new(self.key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv)
    49	    return base64.b64encode(iv + cipher.encrypt(raw))
- AESCipher.decrypt in atm extracts IV from ciphertext (IV is prepended): [repo/atm.py:51-55]
  - /workdir/repo/atm.py lines 51-55:
    51	def decrypt(self, enc):
    52	    enc = base64.b64decode(enc)
    53	    iv = enc[:AES.block_size]
    54	    cipher = AES.new(self.key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv)
    55	    return self._unpad(cipher.decrypt(enc[AES.block_size:])).decode('utf-8')
- Same design in bank (fresh IV per encrypt and IV extracted on decrypt): [repo/bank.py:44-48] and [repo/bank.py:50-54]
  - /workdir/repo/bank.py lines 44-48:
    44	def encrypt(self, raw):
    45	    raw = self._pad(raw)
    46	    iv = Random.new().read(AES.block_size)
    47	    cipher = AES.new(self.key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv)
    48	    return base64.b64encode(iv + cipher.encrypt(raw))
  - /workdir/repo/bank.py lines 50-54:
    50	def decrypt(self, enc):
    51	    enc = base64.b64decode(enc)
    52	    iv = enc[:AES.block_size]
    53	    cipher = AES.new(self.key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv)
    54	    return self._unpad(cipher.decrypt(enc[AES.block_size:])).decode('utf-8')
- Code search results show Random.new().read(AES.block_size) is used to generate the IV in both modules (no other iv assignments or constant IV usage found): grep for "Random.new" in repo returned those lines.

ADDITIONAL NOTES (runtime attempt):
- I attempted a small dynamic test script at /evidence/artifacts/test_iv_freshness.py to encrypt the same plaintext twice and compare IVs, and saved output to /evidence/artifacts/test_iv_output.txt. The dynamic test could not be executed in this environment because the repository is Python 2 code and python2 is not available here. The created files are present:
  - /evidence/artifacts/test_iv_freshness.py (script written)
  - /evidence/artifacts/test_iv_output.txt (contains the failure to run under python3: SyntaxError due to Python2 print statements)

Given the static inspection of the encryption implementation (fresh Random.new().read per encrypt call, IV prepended to ciphertext and extracted on decrypt), there is direct evidence the IV is per-message fresh. Therefore the test PASSes.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The protocol uses a per-request nonce (operation id) which the bank checks and records on receive, but responses are not bound to the request nonce and the ATM does not check any freshness or correlation on receipt. Sensitive values returned in responses (e.g. the new account "card") are accepted by the ATM without any freshness/correlation check, allowing a replayed/forged old response to be accepted. This violates the requirement that any freshness carried in responses that is relied upon must be checked.
EVIDENCE: 
- The client/ATM generates and sends a per-operation id: [/workdir/repo/atm.py:365-376] (atm sets operation["id"] = id_generator(64) and sends the operation).
  - [/workdir/repo/atm.py:365-376] shows main() adding operation["id"] and calling startAtm.
- The bank enforces and records the operation id (replay protection) when receiving requests: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:200-204].
  - [/workdir/repo/bank.py:200-204] checks if operation["id"] is in OpHist and then appends it, preventing replay of requests.
- The bank's responses do NOT include the operation id nor any freshness value: response objects are constructed without any id or nonce and returned directly: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:206-224].
  - In particular, lines [/workdir/repo/bank.py:206-217] build response payloads (card, balance, code) with no operation id.
  - The response is encrypted and sent as-is by the server handler: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:323-325].
- The ATM (response receiver) decrypts and accepts response values (e.g. "card" or "balance") without checking freshness or that the response matches the original request id: [/workdir/repo/atm.py:328-346] and [/workdir/repo/atm.py:330-341].
  - [/workdir/repo/atm.py:328-336] decrypts and parses the response JSON but does not verify any id.
  - [/workdir/repo/atm.py:336-346] accepts response["card"] and writes the card file when code==0 and mode=="n" with no correlation to the sent operation id.
- Because responses lack any freshness/correlation data and the ATM does not validate any freshness on responses, a previously observed response can be replayed and will be accepted by the ATM (e.g. overwriting or creating the card file). This directly matches the failing condition: "Response value nonce not checked".

Files and relevant line ranges (for independent verification):
- /workdir/repo/atm.py:328-346 (response decryption and acceptance, no freshness check)
- /workdir/repo/atm.py:365-376 (operation["id"] generation)
- /workdir/repo/bank.py:176-188 (parsing & digest check of incoming message)
- /workdir/repo/bank.py:200-204 (operation id replay check and recording)
- /workdir/repo/bank.py:206-224 (response construction — no id included)
- /workdir/repo/bank.py:323-325 (server sends encrypted response)

Based on the above concrete code evidence, the test fails because responses carrying security-relevant values are not bound to request freshness nor checked by the response receiver.

(Lines: superData["data"]=..., superData["sec"]=hashlib.sha256(...).hexdigest(), data = cripto.encrypt(data), sock.sendall(...)).
- Bank verifies that same unkeyed checksum (not a keyed MAC): [repo/bank.py:176-186] (processOperation) recomputes digest = hashlib.sha256(superData["data"]).hexdigest() and compares to superData["sec"], i.e. an unkeyed hash is used for integrity/authentication.

These points establish: (1) the protocol uses an unkeyed SHA-256 digest (Unkeyed MAC), and (2) responses are not authenticated/checked by the ATM (No MAC on return). Hence FAIL per the test definition.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The server returns JSON responses whose plaintext length varies with fields that include account name and numeric balance, and those plaintexts are encrypted but then base64-encoded; ciphertext (base64) length is a deterministic function of the padded plaintext length, so an observer can distinguish different balances/account-names by message length. In addition, on protocol errors the server emits an unencrypted literal "protocol_error" response, creating an easily-classifiable plaintext response vs. encrypted success responses.
EVIDENCE: 
- The server builds JSON responses containing balance and code fields (variable-length) and returns them as JSON: [/repo/bank.py:205-224].
- The ServerHandler prints plaintext "protocol_error" on exceptions (unprotected): [/repo/bank.py:312-321].
- The server encrypts the response with AES-CBC and base64-encodes it before sending (so sent length depends on padded plaintext length): AESCipher.encrypt and usage: [/repo/bank.py:38-49] and [/repo/bank.py:323-326].
- The client (atm) similarly encrypts requests with the shared key and expects/decrypts a response — showing the protocol uses encryption+base64 where ciphertext length reveals padded plaintext length: [/repo/atm.py:297-311] and [/repo/atm.py:328-336].

Concrete reasoning from the code:
- AESCipher.encrypt returns base64.b64encode(iv + cipher.encrypt(raw)) meaning the on-wire message length is len(base64(iv||ciphertext)). Ciphertext length is (len(padded_plaintext)) which is a multiple of AES block size plus IV. Thus an observer learning the base64 length can infer the padded plaintext length, and (given JSON structure) infer differences caused by numeric balance length or account name length.
- processOperation places the account/balance into the JSON response for successful balance queries ("balance" key) but sets only {"code":1} on errors; these two cases produce predictably different plaintext lengths and thus predictably different ciphertext lengths.

Because the repository code directly leaks variable-length metadata (and prints an unencrypted protocol_error), this fails the test.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The card secret (cardId) is generated with Python's non-cryptographic random module (random.choice) and stored/transmitted in plaintext. Because id_generator uses the standard PRNG (not Crypto.Random / os.urandom), the secret may be guessable/predictable under realistic attacker models — the implementation does not use a cryptographically secure RNG for card secrets. Therefore the repository fails the requirement that card values be high-entropy and not deterministically derivable.

EVIDENCE:
- The id_generator function uses Python's standard random.choice (non-cryptographic PRNG): [/repo/bank.py:26-27] and duplicated in the client [/repo/atm.py:26-27].
- Accounts set cardId by calling id_generator(16) (card created from the non-crypto RNG): [/repo/bank.py:88-95].
- The bank returns the card value and the ATM writes the card file with that raw value (card file contains only the card secret): ATM writeFile implementation [/repo/atm.py:280-288] and where the ATM writes the card received from the bank [/repo/atm.py:336-340].
- The bank authorizes operations by direct equality of the provided card to the stored cardId (knowing the card string is sufficient to perform balance reads/writes): checks in deposit/withdraw/accountBalance [/repo/bank.py:112-116] and [/repo/bank.py:155-162].
- The bank's auth file (used as AES key) is created with the same insecure id_generator (createAuthFile calls id_generator) [/repo/bank.py:281-293], showing the codebase consistently uses a non-cryptographic RNG for secrets.

These code excerpts are sufficient to demonstrate that card secrets are generated with a predictable PRNG rather than cryptographically secure randomness; therefore the test fails. Recommended fix: generate card secrets with a cryptographically secure RNG (e.g., os.urandom, Crypto.Random) and store/handle them appropriately.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: Static and code-level evidence shows that all ATM->Bank and Bank->ATM network writes use a DataEncryptor (BlowfishDataEncryptor) to encrypt the complete serialized request/response byte arrays before writing to the socket. The request serialization includes account, operation and amount fields; responses include balance/accountKey. Therefore no plaintext sensitive fields are written onto the network (no partial/plaintext sends are present in the reachable code paths).
EVIDENCE: 
- Client-side sends: ATM serializes the full request (transaction, signature, timestamp) and the SocketATM encrypts that entire byte array and writes only the encrypted bytes to the socket: [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/ATMRequest.java:68-83] (ATMRequest.asByteArray builds a string containing the transaction), [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/BankingTransaction.java:38-46] (transaction includes account and amount and operation), and [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/atm/SocketATM.java:41-56] (data = dataEncryptor.encrypt(request.asByteArray()); out.write(data);).
- Server-side receives/decrypts and responds with encrypted response: ServerRequestHandler reads incoming bytes, decrypts, processes, then encrypts the full response byte array and writes only the encrypted bytes: [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/ServerRequestHandler.java:37-43] (decrypt incoming bytes and obtain ATMRequest), [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/BankResponse.java:72-91] (BankResponse.asByteArray includes errorCode, accountKey, balance), and [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/ServerRequestHandler.java:42-57] (byte[] data = dataEncryptor.encrypt(response.asByteArray()); out.write(data);).
- The encryption implementation used is BlowfishDataEncryptor which wraps javax.crypto.Cipher and performs cipher.doFinal on the provided byte[] (i.e. whole payload): [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/BlowfishDataEncryptor.java:35-46] (instance creation) and [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/BlowfishDataEncryptor.java:67-74] (encrypt method does cipher.init(..) and cipher.doFinal(data)).

Notes/observations (verifiable from code):
- All network writes (out.write(...)) in the ATM and ServerRequestHandler are passed the result of DataEncryptor.encrypt(...), so the code path sends only encrypted bytes. There is no code that sends raw transaction/account/balance strings directly over sockets.
- The serialization routines (ATMRequest.asByteArray and BankResponse.asByteArray) include the sensitive fields (account name, operation, amounts, balances), and those serialized bytes are passed to encrypt (full payload encryption), satisfying the requirement that sensitive fields are inside the ciphertext.
- I attempted to compile/run the code to capture runtime traces, but the environment lacked Java toolchain (javac/ant) to execute the program. However the static code evidence above directly shows encryption is invoked on all request/response byte arrays before network transmission.

Files cited (paths and line ranges):
- /repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/atm/SocketATM.java:41-56
- /repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/ServerRequestHandler.java:37-43,54-57
- /repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/ATMRequest.java:68-83
- /repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/BankingTransaction.java:38-46
- /repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/BankResponse.java:72-91
- /repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/BlowfishDataEncryptor.java:35-46,67-74

Given this direct code evidence, the test PASSes: there is encryption applied to the entirety of each request and response payload before sending on the wire, and no plaintext-sensitive bytes are transmitted.
