Fails iff: `No encryption`, `Encryption not on all of request`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The runtime ATM<->Bank communication uses BlowfishDataEncryptor which calls Cipher.getInstance("Blowfish") and initializes the cipher without an IV (cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKey)), i.e. no per-message IV or per-message PRNG seed is provided. This means the cipher operates in a mode with no per-message IV (typically ECB or provider-default) and encryptions are deterministic for a given key—thus the IV/seed is effectively fixed/absent across messages.

EVIDENCE:
- The bank server constructs a BlowfishDataEncryptor for runtime use: [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/SocketServer.java:36-40] shows this.dataEncryptor = BlowfishDataEncryptor.getInstance(authFile, true);
- The ATM client uses BlowfishDataEncryptor for its runtime messages: [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/atm/SocketATM.java:20-24] shows this.dataEncryptor = BlowfishDataEncryptor.getInstance(authFile, false); and [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/atm/SocketATM.java:41-46] shows the encrypted bytes are written directly to the socket.
- Blowfish encrypt/decrypt do not use or generate any IV: [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/BlowfishDataEncryptor.java:35-36] (Cipher.getInstance("Blowfish")) and [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/BlowfishDataEncryptor.java:67-71] (cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKey); return cipher.doFinal(data);). The code never supplies an IvParameterSpec or any per-message randomness to the cipher.

(For contrast: AESDataEncryptor implements per-message IV generation using SecureRandom and prepends the IV to ciphertext: [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/AESDataEncryptor.java:73-87]. However AESDataEncryptor is not used for the ATM<->Bank runtime path.)

metadata.test_description: For every reachable encryption of any atm<->bank runtime message, the IV/seed input to the cipher is not a fixed constant across encryptions (i.e., the IV and IV seed is per-message fresh rather than hardcoded or globally constant). Fails iff: `Fixed IV`, `Fixed IV seed`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The protocol uses a timestamp freshness value (ATMRequest.timestamp) and the server checks it on receipt, but the server does not record accepted timestamps to prevent reuse (nonce/timestamp replay). validateTimestamp only tests freshness and set-membership but never inserts the timestamp into the per-account set, so replays of the same timestamp are accepted. This violates the requirement to track nonces to prevent reuse.
EVIDENCE:
- ATMRequest constructs and transmits an explicit timestamp: [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/ATMRequest.java:22-29] and serializes it into the wire format: [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/ATMRequest.java:68-78].
- The server validates timestamps on receipt: Clearing calls validateTimestamp on incoming requests for authenticated operations: [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Clearing.java:56-62].
- The per-account timestamp validation logic checks age and membership but does not record accepted timestamps (no add/insert): [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Account.java:16-23] (timestamps field init) and [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Account.java:92-100] (validateTimestamp only checks and returns true/false; it never inserts the timestamp into the timestamps set).
- A repo-wide search shows the timestamps set is declared and referenced only in Account.java (no code adds timestamps), so reuse tracking is absent: the only occurrences are the declaration/init and contains() check in Account.java.

Consequence: Since accepted timestamps are not recorded, an attacker who observes a valid signed request can replay it (same timestamp/signature) and the server will accept it as long as it still falls within the time window, resulting in a replay vulnerability. This is a direct failure of the test criterion requiring nonces/timestamps to be tracked to prevent reuse.

metadata.test_description: For every reachable security-relevant request/response exchange, the protocol uses an explicit freshness value (nonce/timestamp) when required, and receivers enforce freshness on all acceptance paths by validating it on receipt (including return/error paths), bounding it (no overflow / overly-large windows), and tracking it to prevent reuse; additionally, any freshness carried in responses that is relied upon by the protocol is also checked. Fails iff: `No nonce used`, `Nonce not checked on receive`, `Nonces not checked`, `Nonces not recorded`, `Response value nonce not checked`, `Nonce overflows`, `Timestamp window too large for nonce`, `Ignore check failure`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: Bank-to-ATM responses (including success and error responses that affect ATM control flow/state) are not protected by a keyed MAC and are not checked by the ATM. The repository only signs ATM->Bank requests with an HMAC; Bank responses are serialized, encrypted with Blowfish, and sent without any MAC/authentication tag and the ATM does not verify any MAC on responses.
EVIDENCE:
- ATMRequest contains an HMAC signature on requests (ATM->Bank): [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/ATMRequest.java:22-29] and the HMAC implementation is in [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/HMACDataSigner.java:57-66] and verification on the bank side is performed in Clearing: [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Clearing.java:56-58].

- Bank responses (BankResponse) have no MAC/signature field when serialized: [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/BankResponse.java:72-92] (asByteArray) and parsing from bytes has no authentication step: [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/BankResponse.java:50-69] .

- The server sends responses by encrypting the raw BankResponse bytes and writing them to the socket (no MAC added): [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/ServerRequestHandler.java:42-46].

- The ATM receives and decrypts the server response and directly parses BankResponse.fromByteArray(...) without any MAC verification: [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/atm/SocketATM.java:56-58].

- Error responses are produced by Clearing on verification/other failures (e.g. response = new BankResponse(255)) and these are also sent without any MAC: [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Clearing.java:88-97] together with the server send-site above [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/ServerRequestHandler.java:42-46].

Together these show that while ATM->Bank requests are HMAC-signed and the bank verifies them, Bank->ATM responses (including error responses that affect ATM control flow/state) are not MACed and the ATM performs no MAC verification on any return path. This violates the requirement that acceptance on all paths be conditioned on verifying a keyed MAC.

metadata.test_description: For every reachable attacker-controllable atm<->bank runtime message that can influence control flow or state, acceptance is conditioned on verifying a keyed message-authentication tag, and that verification is enforced on all acceptance paths (including return/error paths). Fails iff: `No MAC`, `No MAC on return`, `Unkeyed MAC`, `MAC not checked for error response`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The server's response serialization and use of non-length-hiding encryptors makes success vs failure (and some success types) have predictable different message lengths; an observer can use message length metadata to infer account-related fields (e.g., created account keys or balances that cross block boundaries). The repo also contains a DummyDataEncryptor that returns plaintext unchanged (fully leaking lengths) and the server uses BlowfishDataEncryptor by default (ciphertext length depends on plaintext length and padding).
EVIDENCE: 
- Response format shows account key / balance included in plaintext and serialized as: errorCode;accountKeyBase64_or_null;balance_or_null — see BankResponse.asByteArray implementation [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/BankResponse.java:72-91] and parsing [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/BankResponse.java:50-69].
- Error vs success construction in executeTransaction: errors set response = new BankResponse(255); success cases sometimes include an account key (CREATE_ACCOUNT) or a balance (BALANCE) which change the serialized length [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Clearing.java:65-83] and error handling [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Clearing.java:88-97].
- Server uses a DataEncryptor but writes the encrypted bytes directly to the socket without any length-hiding or fixed-size framing; the handler encrypts response.asByteArray() and writes it as-is [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/ServerRequestHandler.java:42-46].
- Default server chooses BlowfishDataEncryptor (no IV prefix) in SocketServer start-up: BlowfishDataEncryptor.getInstance(...) is used by default [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/SocketServer.java:36-40]. Blowfish encryptor produces ciphertext whose length is a function of the plaintext length (padded to the block size) [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/BlowfishDataEncryptor.java:1-33, 47-56, 58-69]. AES option (AESDataEncryptor) prepends a per-message IV and still results in ciphertext length dependent on plaintext length modulo blocksize [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/AESDataEncryptor.java:73-88].
- There is a DummyDataEncryptor that returns plaintext unchanged (fully leaking message lengths) [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/DummyDataEncryptor.java:30-36].
- Runtime evidence (artifacts): I compiled and ran small tests that construct BankResponse objects and measured plaintext and encrypted lengths. These outputs demonstrate: (1) plaintext responses differ between error and balance shapes and between error and account-creation; (2) the dummy encryptor leaks plaintext lengths directly; (3) Blowfish ciphertext length varies between response types (e.g. create-account ciphertext larger than error ciphertext). Saved outputs:
  - /evidence/artifacts/TestLength.out (shows plaintext and ciphertext lengths for an error and two balances; and dummy encryptor leakage)
  - /evidence/artifacts/TestVarlen.out (iterated many balance values showing plaintext length changes; Blowfish ciphertext remained 16 bytes for small balances but plaintext lengths vary — demonstrating information is present before encryption)
  - /evidence/artifacts/TestAccountKey.out (shows a CREATE_ACCOUNT-like response with an account key: plaintext length=31 and ciphertext length=32, distinct from error ciphertext length=16)

- [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/BankResponse.java:72-91]
- [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/BankResponse.java:50-69]
- [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Clearing.java:65-83]

- [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/ServerRequestHandler.java:42-46]
- [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/SocketServer.java:36-40]
- [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/DummyDataEncryptor.java:30-36]

- [/workdir/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/AESDataEncryptor.java:73-88]

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The bank server decrypts incoming requests using a per-instance DataEncryptor and then the clearing logic explicitly rejects requests whose credentials fail verification or whose timestamps are invalid; privileged state-changing actions (create/withdraw/deposit/balance) are only executed after these checks succeed. Failed decryption or signature/timestamp verification results in an error response and no privileged effect.
EVIDENCE:
- Server performs channel decryption before parsing the request: [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/ServerRequestHandler.java:37-40] (reads encryptedRequest, calls dataEncryptor.decrypt(...), then ATMRequest.fromByteArray(...)). If any exception occurs the handler writes "protocol_error" and does not forward the request for execution [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/ServerRequestHandler.java:49-52].
- The server-side clearing enforces credential verification and timestamp checks before performing actions: signature verification and timestamp validation are performed and throw on failure [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Clearing.java:56-63].
- Privileged effects (account insert, deposit, withdraw, balance reporting) occur only later in the code path after the checks (switch executing actions) [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Clearing.java:65-84]. If verification or other argument checks fail, an IllegalArgumentException is caught and the bank returns an error response (255) and does not perform privileged actions [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Clearing.java:88-93].
- The HMAC-based verifier implementation compares the computed signature to the provided signature (byte equality) [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/HMACDataSigner.java:71-73], proving that signature failures will be detected.
- The server and client are configured to use a shared Blowfish DataEncryptor (server creates/loads key with getInstance(authFile, true) when starting, and the ATM client loads the same key with getInstance(authFile, false)), demonstrating that incoming requests are expected to be encrypted with the channel key [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/SocketServer.java:36-39] and [repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/atm/SocketATM.java:20-23,41-46].

These code locations provide direct, verifiable evidence that (1) the communication is decrypted before processing, and (2) transaction execution is gated on successful credential verification (HMAC) and timestamp validation; therefore requests with missing/failed credentials cannot trigger privileged effects.  (Replay/tampering protections are out of scope as stated.)

metadata.test_description: For every privileged-action execution event, the action executes only if the communication channel is authenticated and the request includes credentials that are present and verified; requests with missing/failed credentials cannot trigger privileged effects. (Replay/tampering of previously authenticated traffic is out of scope for this property.) Fails iff: `Unauthenticated client`.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: Card secrets are generated using a cryptographic KeyGenerator producing a 256-bit HMAC key (random) and stored as a binary card file. The code does not derive card secrets from the account name or any other public identifier; verification uses the stored random key. Therefore card secrets are high-entropy, not deterministically derived, and not guessable from account identifiers.
EVIDENCE:
- Card secret is created by calling DataSigner.generateKey() in the Account constructor (random key assigned to account): [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Account.java:41-46]
- The concrete implementation HMACDataSigner.generateKey() uses javax.crypto.KeyGenerator initialized for "HmacSHA256" with KEY_LENGTH=256 and returns keyGen.generateKey().getEncoded() (i.e., a 256-bit random key): [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/crypto/HMACDataSigner.java:47-51]
- When a new account is created, the bank returns the account key to the ATM and the ATM saves the raw account key bytes to the card file via FileHandler.saveBinaryFile(...): [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/atm/ATM.java:101-103] and [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/common/FileHandler.java:43-51]
- The bank verifies requests by checking the HMAC signature using the account's stored card secret (account.getCardSecret()) — i.e., the key used for verification is the generated random key, not a hash of the account name: [/repo/src/java/bibifi/sphericalcow/bank/Clearing.java:52-57]
Notes: I inspected the repository source to find how card secrets are generated, returned, saved, and used for verification. There is no code that constructs card secrets by hashing or otherwise deterministically deriving them from the account name or other public identifier. Based on the evidence above, the test condition "no exploitable vulnerability due to guessable/derivable card secrets" PASSes.

EVIDENCE:
- The request includes sensitive fields Account, Card, Action and Val when marshaled: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/marshal.go:12-19] and unmarshalled on the server side: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/marshal.go:31-38].
- The client writes the marshaled request bytes directly to the connection: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/client.go:22-31] (MarshalRequest then conn.Write).
- The server reads bytes from the connection and unmarshals the request: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:27-36] (conn.Read then UnmarshalRequest).
- The ATM binary establishes a TLS connection to the bank before creating the protocol client: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/atm/atm.go:61-65] (tls.DialWithDialer is used and its tls.Config is provided).
- The Bank binary listens with TLS and accepts connections from the tls.Listener, passing the accepted conn to the RPC handler: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/bank/bank.go:55-58] and [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/bank/bank.go:66-75] (tls.Listen and ln.Accept -> rpc.Handle(conn)).

Notes / caveats: The code uses TLS for the runtime path implemented by the provided atm and bank commands, so network bytes are encrypted by TLS. tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository does not use any hardcoded or global IV/seed for atm<->bank message encryption. Transport encryption is handled by Go's crypto/tls (see client/server TLS setup), and TLS session keys/certificates are generated using crypto/rand. I found no code that sets a fixed IV or seed for encryption.

EVIDENCE:
- The ATM client sets up a TLS connection (so encryption is performed by crypto/tls), and specifies cipher suites in code: [repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/atm/atm.go:61-65] shows the tls.DialWithDialer call and CipherSuites configuration (line 64 sets CipherSuites). This demonstrates encryption is performed by the standard TLS library (not an ad-hoc cipher with a hardcoded IV).
- The Bank server similarly uses crypto/tls to listen for connections and sets CipherSuites: [repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/bank/bank.go:55-58]. The server constructs certificates and passes them to tls.Listen (so the TLS handshake/key derivation is used for each connection).
- Certificate/key material is generated with cryptographically secure randomness: [repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/auth/keys.go:17-24,32-34,57] uses crypto/rand (rand.Reader and rand.Int) and rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader, ...). This shows per-run randomness for keys/serial numbers used in TLS handshakes.
- Runtime artifact: I started the bank and saved the generated certificate (server cert) to an evidence file; it contains a random serial number (showing the cert/key are freshly created rather than fixed). See [/evidence/artifacts/cert1.txt] (file contains the certificate text and Serial Number field). The presence of a per-run random certificate implies the handshake secrets (and therefore derived keys/IVs/nonces) are not globally constant.
- I searched the codebase for any explicit IV/nonce/seed assignment and found no application code that sets a fixed IV for encryption (aside from unrelated local variables in protobuf internals). Grep for iv/IV/nonce/seed produced no results indicating a hardcoded IV in the ATM<->Bank protocol implementation.

Notes/clarification:
- The repository relies on Go's crypto/tls to perform network encryption. Modern TLS versions and Go's implementation derive per-connection key material and per-record nonces from secure randomness generated during the handshake; there is no fixed global IV or seed in the application code.
- The server code restricts CipherSuites to TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA in the tls.Config, but TLS negotiation and the Go library behavior may select an appropriate negotiated cipher/version. Regardless, there is no use of a hardcoded IV/seed in application code.

If you want further runtime evidence (for example TLS ConnectionState details such as negotiated CipherSuite or per-connection randomness), I can modify the client/server code to print tls.ConnectionState after handshake and save that output under /evidence/artifacts/.

REASON: The ATM<->Bank messages are transported over TLS with peer authentication (ATM validates server cert) and a cipher suite that provides a keyed MAC (TLS record HMAC). Thus every attacker-controllable message in both directions is integrity-protected and authenticity-checked by the TLS layer before application code accepts or acts on it; read/write failures (including MAC failures) are handled as errors and cause the server/client to abort without accepting the message or to roll back transactions.

EVIDENCE:
- TLS client setup (ATM verifies server cert via RootCAs): [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/atm/atm.go:61-66] shows tls.DialWithDialer used with RootCAs set, which enforces certificate validation and establishes a TLS session that provides keyed MAC protection for records.
- TLS server setup (Bank uses TLS listener with server certificate): [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/bank/bank.go:46-58] shows the server creating a certificate and calling tls.Listen, establishing a TLS-protected listener.
- No application-layer MAC fields in the protocol: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/marshal.go:12-19] and [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/marshal.go:41-45] show Request/Response protobufs are marshaled without any explicit MAC/tag field (i.e., integrity is provided at transport layer).
- Application only processes messages after reading from the TLS connection and unmarshalling; read/unmarshal errors are treated as protocol errors and the handler returns without accepting: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:27-40].
- rpcReply write errors are handled and will cause rollback if appropriate; failed writes (which would include transport integrity failures) result in protocol_error and transaction rollback when needed: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:70-77] and successful commit only happens when no error: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:80-83].

Notes / Clarification: The repository does not implement an application-layer MAC (the protobuf Request/Response structs have no MAC field), but the transport uses TLS (cipher suite TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA) which provides an HMAC-based record authentication using session keys. This satisfies the requirement that acceptance be conditioned on verification of a keyed MAC, because the TLS layer will detect and return errors on MAC failures before application code unmarshals or processes messages, and the application handles such errors by aborting/rolling-back. VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The protocol's serialized response length is directly and predictably dependent on the numeric value of the account balance (the Val field). The code always marshals a Response {Val, HasError} using protobuf varint encoding, so the wire-length of the response grows with the magnitude of Val. An observer (MITM) can use the observed response length to infer ranges of account balances. This violates the test (predictable response length leaking balance).

EVIDENCE:
1) Response structure (shows the encoded fields that determine wire length): [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/serial/serial.proto:19-21]
   - Response has `required uint64 val = 1;` and `required bool hasError = 2;` (both encoded as varints). The uint64 varint length depends on the numeric value.

2) Response marshaling (the code always marshals Val and HasError into the wire format): [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/marshal.go:41-45]
   - MarshalResponse calls proto.Marshal on serial.Response{Val: res.Val, HasError: res.HasError}.

3) Where Val is set (on success) vs left at zero (on error): [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:61-68]
   - The code only assigns res.Val when txErr == nil via res.Val, err = tx.Exec(). On error, res.Val remains zero and res.HasError is true. Thus success vs error and the returned numeric value control the wire encoding.

4) rpcReply writes the marshaled bytes directly to the connection (so the attacker can observe message length): [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:86-93]
   - rpcReply writes the proto bytes with conn.Write(data) without any length padding or masking.

5) Concrete computed examples (varint/protobuf wire encodings and lengths) demonstrating that response length increases with Val magnitude. See generated artifact with sample values and resulting message lengths: /evidence/artifacts/lengths.txt
   - Example excerpt (from /evidence/artifacts/lengths.txt):
     hasError= False
     val=           0 len= 4 bytes=08001000
     val=         127 len= 4 bytes=087f1000
     val=         128 len= 5 bytes=0880011000
     val=       16384 len= 6 bytes=088080011000
   - This shows length changes from 4 to 5 to 6 bytes as Val crosses varint boundaries.

Technical note (why this leaks): protobuf encodes uint64 as a varint (7 bits per byte). The total response size is: 1 byte (field-key for val) + varint_length(val) + 1 byte (field-key for hasError) + 1 byte (varint for boolean) = 3 + varint_length(val). Thus observing the total message length reveals varint_length(val), which gives a range for Val (e.g., len=4 => val < 128, len=5 => 128 <= val < 16384, etc.).

Conclusion: The repository fails the test because message length (an observable metadata) is predictably correlated with account balance. The code does not pad, normalize, or otherwise mask response lengths or protect connection metadata that would prevent such inference.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The bank server does not enforce client authentication on the communication channel and allows at least one privileged action (account creation) to execute without requiring verified credentials in the request. Although some actions (Deposit/Withdraw/Balance) verify card credentials, the server accepts TLS connections without requiring client-authentication and does not inspect connection authentication state; furthermore MakeAccount (account creation) does not verify any credential before creating the account.
EVIDENCE: 
- Server binds a TLS listener but does not require or verify client authentication: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/bank/bank.go:52-58] shows tls.Listen configured only with server Certificates and CipherSuites (no ClientAuth or request for client certs).
- RPC handler reads requests and dispatches actions without checking connection auth state: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:21-41] (request unmarshal) and [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:44-59] (dispatch to actions).
- MakeAccount does not verify credentials from the request; it constructs a new account from the provided Card field and returns a transaction directly: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:100-114]. This means an unauthenticated client (one that did not present or have verified credentials) can cause account creation.
- By contrast, operations that act on existing accounts do verify the card credential: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/bank/bank.go:31-44] (GetAccount returns BadCard if cardData != stored card). Thus credential verification exists for some actions but is absent for MakeAccount.
- Client-side code (ATM) performs server certificate validation by loading the server auth file into RootCAs, which is a client-side check and does not substitute for server-enforced client authentication: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/atm/atm.go:50-56] and [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/atm/atm.go:61-65].

Together these show privileged effects (account creation) can be triggered without verified credentials and that the server does not enforce client authentication — therefore the test fails with the failure mode `Unauthenticated client`.

Protobuf unmarshal (generated) code performs length and EOF checks and returns errors on malformed/short data; rpc.Handle logs and returns when unmarshal or read errors occur; transactions are rolled back on reply failures and locks are released via Confirm/Rollback methods. Input-parsing helpers also validate sizes. I found no code paths where attacker-controlled input can cause unchecked indexing or uncaught panics that would disrupt protocol integrity.

EVIDENCE:
- Server request read and error handling: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:24-41] shows the server reads into a fixed buffer, checks Read errors, calls UnmarshalRequest, and returns on error.
- Response write and rollback on error: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:70-78] shows rpcReply errors trigger tx.Rollback() and return, preventing inconsistent state. rpcReply itself checks write length: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:86-95].
- Client read/write error handling: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/client.go:21-42] shows the client checks write/read errors and returns errors from UnmarshalResponse instead of panicking.
- Protobuf unmarshal performs robust bounds/length checks and returns errors on malformed or truncated input (prevents unchecked slicing/indexing). See generated code checking lengths and EOF at multiple points, e.g. string/bytes length checks and postIndex bounds: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/serial/serial.pb.go:261-321] and [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/serial/serial.pb.go:340-349] and the final required-field checks [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/serial/serial.pb.go:404-421].
- Transaction semantics ensure locks are always released and rollbacks undo partial state changes: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/bank/transaction.go:18-37] and [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/bank/transaction.go:45-63] show Exec/Confirm/Rollback patterns.
- Input validation for account/file lengths and character sets to prevent oversized/malformed fields: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/parse/validate.go:13-19] and [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/parse/validate.go:21-31].

All cited evidence exists in the repository and demonstrates defensive checks at parsing boundaries, error propagation, and transaction rollback/cleanup. No uncaught exceptions or unchecked packet-size-dependent operations were found on reachable network paths. VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository generates card secrets with crypto/rand (high entropy 16 bytes) and uses those card bytes verbatim for authentication; there is no code that deterministically derives the card from the account name (no hashing or deterministic derivation). Therefore an MITM cannot compute card secrets from public identifiers.
EVIDENCE:
- Random high-entropy card generation: NewCard uses crypto/rand to fill 16 bytes via rand.Read, producing cryptographically strong randomness. [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/bank/card.go:1-9]
- Card file written and read as raw 16-byte secret (created by NewCard and saved as the card file; readCard enforces length == 16): [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/atm/atm.go:73-79] and [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/cmd/atm/atm.go:96-113]
- Server uses the provided card bytes directly for account creation and authentication (card is stored on account creation and later compared bytewise; authentication compares card equality, not recomputing from account name): account creation/store: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/bank/bank.go:16-24] and account auth comparison: [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/bank/bank.go:31-41]
- RPC layer passes the client's card through without deriving it from public identifiers (MakeAccount/Deposit/Withdraw/Balance all accept req.Card): [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:1-22] and [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:56-92] and [/repo/src/bitbucket.org/neilvallon/bibifi/protocol/rpc.go:101-138]

I searched the repository for uses of hashing or deterministic derivation related to cards (e.g., sha/md5/hash/HMAC) and found no code that derives a card from the account name; instead the card is produced by NewCard with crypto/rand and transported/stored as raw 16 bytes. Based on these artifacts, the test passes.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository implements explicit nonces for the security-relevant request/response exchanges (the /nonce handshake and the main transaction POST). The server generates, stores and bounds nonces, the server enforces freshness and prevents reuse by popping stored nonces on first use, and both sides verify message authenticity (HMAC + encryption) on responses that carry nonces. On validation failure the server rejects the request (error path).

EVIDENCE:
- Server generates and records nonces: [/repo/src/bank.py:35-38] (get_nonce sets __nonces[nonce] = datetime.now() and returns nonce).
  - [/repo/src/bank.py:35-38]
- Server enforces freshness and bounds nonce lifetime: [/repo/src/bank.py:40-48] (test_nonce pops creation time and compares elapsed_sec > __nonce_duration_sec, raising on invalid/expired nonces).
  - [/repo/src/bank.py:40-48]
- Server prevents reuse by removing the nonce when checking: [/repo/src/bank.py:50-55] (get_nonce_created pops the nonce from __nonces under a lock).
  - [/repo/src/bank.py:50-55]
- Server validates nonce before processing the main transaction endpoint and returns an error on failure: [/repo/src/bank.py:166-176, 196-203] (handle_transaction calls test_nonce(env['HTTP_NONCE']) for PATH_INFO '/' and exceptions cause request_error which returns 500).
  - [/repo/src/bank.py:166-176]
  - [/repo/src/bank.py:196-203]
- Server returns the nonce to clients over the /nonce endpoint and authenticates that response (MAC + encryption): [/repo/src/bank.py:180-187] (the /nonce branch calls test_mac on the request, calls get_nonce(), then prepare_payload to set MAC and IV headers in the response).
  - [/repo/src/bank.py:180-187]
- Client requests nonce and checks authenticity of the response before using it, and includes the nonce in the subsequent transaction request: [/repo/src/atm.py:33-43, 49-56] (request_nonce reads response, checks MAC with test_mac and decrypts; perform_request sets headers['NONCE'] = nonce then POSTs to '/').
  - [/repo/src/atm.py:33-43]
  - [/repo/src/atm.py:49-56]
- Nonce lifetime is explicitly small (2 seconds): [/repo/src/bank.py:21] (__nonce_duration_sec = 2) — this demonstrates an explicit bound is used.
  - [/repo/src/bank.py:21]

Notes/limitations (for reproducibility):
- The static code evidence above shows the intended freshness design (nonce generation, storage, bounded lifetime, pop-on-check to avoid reuse, and rejection on failure). I did not run the code; if you want runtime confirmation (e.g., to ensure the code paths execute as written in your environment) I can run the server and client to produce request logs and demonstrate nonce acceptance/rejection. However, the static source lines cited are direct, verifiable evidence of nonce generation and checking in the protocol.

Given the direct, verifiable code evidence that nonces are used, checked on receive, bounded, tracked to prevent reuse, and that responses carrying nonces are authenticated before use, I judge the test PASS.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: Both ATM and bank attach and verify a keyed HMAC on all request and successful-response messages that can change control flow or state. The bank verifies incoming MACs before decrypting/accepting requests; the ATM verifies MACs on responses before decrypting/accepting them. Error responses from the bank do not include a MAC, but the ATM does not accept non-200 responses (and would abort if MAC is missing), so no acceptance path exists that bypasses keyed-MAC verification for state-changing messages.
EVIDENCE: 
- Keyed HMAC implementation: shared.py defines make_hmac and check_hmac using a secret key (HMAC): [/repo/src/shared.py:15-35].
- ATM sends MAC header on requests to bank (nonce request): ATM sets 'MAC' header when calling /nonce: [/repo/src/atm.py:37-38].
- ATM verifies MAC on /nonce response before using it: [/repo/src/atm.py:41-43].
- ATM sends MAC header on transaction requests and verifies MAC on transaction responses: ATM prepares payload with MAC and then verifies response MAC: [/repo/src/atm.py:26-31] and [/repo/src/atm.py:67-71].
- Bank verifies MACs on incoming requests before decrypting/accepting: decrypt_payload calls test_mac which checks MAC using the server HMAC key: [/repo/src/bank.py:162-165] and [/repo/src/bank.py:57-60].
- Bank includes a keyed MAC on successful (200) responses: prepare_payload sets the HTTP 'MAC' header using make_hmac: [/repo/src/bank.py:154-159].
- The code paths that change server state are perform_transaction (create/deposit/withdraw) and are reached only after decrypting and MAC verification: [/repo/src/bank.py:127-144] and [/repo/src/bank.py:167-179].
- Bank error response does not include a MAC (request_error sends 500 with empty headers), but ATM treats non-200 responses as errors and will not accept them (and would fail MAC checks if headers were missing): [/repo/src/bank.py:30-34] and [/repo/src/atm.py:64-66] and [/repo/src/atm.py:41-43].

All of the above are reproducible by inspecting the listed files. Based on this evidence, the repository enforces keyed MAC verification on all acceptance paths for messages that influence control flow or state, so the test PASSes.

tests.description:
VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The bank server enforces authentication checks (HMAC and nonce) at all entry points before executing privileged actions. Requests for /nonce require a valid MAC, and requests to / require a valid (recent) NONCE and a valid MAC over the encrypted payload; failures raise exceptions and are mapped to request_error (HTTP 500) so perform_transaction is never reached. Therefore privileged effects (create/deposit/withdraw/balance) cannot be triggered by requests with missing or invalid credentials.

EVIDENCE:
- Authentication and request-rejection logic in the server (enforced before performing transactions):
  - /repo/src/bank.py:167-181  (handle_transaction: transaction path '/') — shows test_nonce(env['HTTP_NONCE']) then decrypt_payload then json.loads(payload) then perform_transaction(command).
  - /repo/src/bank.py:182-187  (handle_transaction: '/nonce') — shows test_mac(env, payload) is required to get a nonce.
  - /repo/src/bank.py:162-165  (decrypt_payload) — calls test_mac(env, payload) and decrypt; invalid MAC causes exception.
  - /repo/src/bank.py:40-50   (test_nonce) — validates nonce existence and expiry; get_nonce_created pops nonces so replay without a fresh nonce fails.
  - /repo/src/bank.py:30-33   (request_error) and /repo/src/bank.py:192-194 (exception handler in handle_transaction) — exceptions result in request_error (HTTP 500) and do not call perform_transaction.

- HMAC verification is strict and fails fast:
  - /repo/src/shared.py:15-25 (make_hmac) — creates HMAC over message using the shared key.
  - /repo/src/shared.py:27-35 (check_hmac) — compares provided and computed HMAC and raises ValueError on mismatch.

- Privileged actions are only reached after these checks:
  - /repo/src/bank.py:127-152 (perform_transaction) — actual privileged operations (do_create, do_deposit, do_withdraw, get_balance) are invoked only from handle_transaction after successful nonce and MAC/decryption checks.

ATTEMPTED DYNAMIC VERIFICATION (saved logs):
- I attempted to start the server to run an end-to-end test; the direct script execution initially failed due to missing import lines in the repository. I applied minimal imports to allow module resolution but the server still failed to start in this environment; the server startup attempt produced a runtime log saved at /evidence/artifacts/server.log showing the failure (NameError). This does not affect the static code evidence above which clearly shows authentication gating. The log is available here:
  - /evidence/artifacts/server.log

CONCLUSION: Static and code-path evidence demonstrates that privileged actions are only executed after a valid nonce and valid HMAC authentication; requests with missing or invalid credentials are rejected and cannot trigger privileged effects. Therefore the test PASSes.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository contains reachable runtime code paths that produce uncaught exceptions and missing validations. Running the server script fails immediately due to missing references (unhandled NameError), the WSGI handler re-raises lower-level errors (which can crash/terminate request handling), and request body reads are performed without any size checks. These issues allow attacker-influenced inputs (malformed requests, oversized bodies, missing headers) to trigger exceptions or resource exhaustion and disrupt protocol integrity.

EVIDENCE:
1) Immediate runtime crash when attempting to run the bank server: captured traceback showing NameError due to missing/undefined names (server cannot start): [/evidence/artifacts/run_bank_output.txt]. The file contains the observed traceback produced when running the server script (see file). This demonstrates an uncaught exception during startup that impacts protocol integrity.

2) bank.py references ModifiedOptionParser and general_error but does not import shared.py, causing NameError at runtime. Evidence of reference and exception:
   - Reference to ModifiedOptionParser in bank.py (no import present): [/workdir/repo/src/bank.py:237-247] (line 240: p = ModifiedOptionParser()).
   - Definition of ModifiedOptionParser exists in shared.py, showing it was likely intended to be used but not imported: [/workdir/repo/src/shared.py:68-71].
   (Because bank.py does not import shared.py, these definitions are not available and cause NameError.)

3) Missing import / NameError inside shared.py: generate_nonce uses base64 but shared.py does not import base64. This would raise NameError when generate_nonce is invoked (attacker-controlled nonce request): [/workdir/repo/src/shared.py:37-39].

4) The HTTP request handling performs unbounded reads and re-raises low-level errors in the WSGI handler:
   - handle_transaction reads request body without any size limit: env['wsgi.input'].read() at [/workdir/repo/src/bank.py:167-174] (line 171). This allows an attacker to send very large payloads to cause resource exhaustion or other unexpected behavior.
   - The custom WSGI handler catches exceptions, calls protocol_error(), then re-raises the exception: [/workdir/repo/src/bank.py:195-203]. Re-raising can let the exception propagate to the server/worker and may terminate or disrupt request handling.

5) HMAC/Header assumptions without presence checks: test_mac and decrypt_payload access headers like env['HTTP_MAC'] and env['HTTP_IV'] directly (no membership checks) leading to KeyError if the attacker omits or malforms headers. These calls are in decrypt_payload and test_mac: [/workdir/repo/src/bank.py:57-59] and [/workdir/repo/src/bank.py:162-165]. VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The "card" value is deterministically derived as an HMAC of the account name (no per-card randomness). The ATM creates the card as make_hmac(account, hmac_key) and the bank validates the card by recomputing the same HMAC; the card file contains only this deterministic HMAC string (no randomness). This matches the failing conditions: "No randomness in card file" and "Card is hash of account name." 
EVIDENCE: 
- Card creation: the ATM creates the card contents as an HMAC of the account name: [/repo/src/atm.py:127-130] shows create_card_file_contents uses make_hmac(account, hmac_key) and returns that value.
- Card validation: the bank validates the card by recomputing the HMAC over the account using the server HMAC key: [/repo/src/bank.py:123-125] (validate_card uses make_hmac(payload['account'], __hmac_key) and compares to payload['card']).
- HMAC implementation: shared.make_hmac uses HMAC-MD5 and deterministically returns a hex digest of the message keyed by the secret: [/repo/src/shared.py:15-25].

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: All ATM->Bank and Bank->ATM runtime messages that carry sensitive fields are placed into a single string, encrypted with AES, base64-encoded, and sent as the value of the HTTP form field "transaction" (so no plaintext sensitive fields are placed on the wire). The bank reads that same "transaction" field and decrypts it before processing, and all responses that carry sensitive fields are also encrypted before being written to the HTTP response.

EVIDENCE:
- ATM constructs the sensitive payload (action, account, balance/amount, pin, nonce, timestamp, hash), encrypts it, and sends it in the POST form field named "transaction": [/repo/atm.py:111-118] (payload creation + enc_data = cy.encrypt(data) and form = {'transaction':enc_data}; urllib.urlencode(form) and urllib2.Request).
  - Examples for other operations show the same pattern (encrypt then form['transaction']): [/repo/atm.py:163-170] (deposit) and [/repo/atm.py:206-213] (withdraw).
- Bank reads the POST form field "transaction" and immediately decrypts it before extracting sensitive fields: [/repo/bank.py:226-231] (cypheredData = form["transaction"].value; aesCypher = AESCipher(bank.key); decypheredData = aesCypher.decrypt(cypheredData); fieldList = extractFields(decypheredData)).
- Bank responses that include sensitive fields (e.g., balance) are encrypted before being written to the HTTP response body: [/repo/bank.py:260-263] (initial_balance response encrypted), [/repo/bank.py:272-275] (deposit response encrypted), [/repo/bank.py:281-284] (balance response encrypted), [/repo/bank.py:299-303] (withdraw response encrypted), and error responses are encrypted as well [/repo/bank.py:309-317].

These file excerpts are present in the repository and show that the protocol places all sensitive request/response fields inside ciphertext values exchanged over HTTP, so no plaintext sensitive bytes are transmitted in the request/response bodies.

Notes/Limitations (for completeness):
- The code uses plain HTTP (not TLS), but sensitive fields are encrypted at application layer (AES) before being put into the HTTP body. The test condition only requires that bytes carrying sensitive fields on the network be encrypted; this repo satisfies that by encrypting payloads into the "transaction" field.  
- No dynamic execution was necessary to confirm the transmissions because the code statically constructs and parses the same encrypted field on both sides; the cited lines show both sides consistently use the encrypted field.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: Both the ATM and Bank AESCipher.encrypt implementations generate a fresh IV per encryption using Crypto.Random.new().read(AES.block_size). There are no occurrences of a hardcoded or global fixed IV or any explicit seeding of the RNG in the repository, so IV/seed is per-message fresh.
EVIDENCE: 
- ATM AESCipher.encrypt: uses Random.new().read(AES.block_size) to produce IV per call [/repo/atm.py:36-44].
- Bank AESCipher.encrypt: uses Random.new().read(AES.block_size) to produce IV per call [/repo/bank.py:159-166].
- Search for other IV/seed assignments shows no other fixed IV or RNG seeding (the only iv assignments are the per-call reads and iv extraction from ciphertext) [repo/atm.py:41,47; repo/bank.py:164,170].

You can verify by inspecting the cited lines in the repository: both encrypt() implementations prepend iv to the ciphertext and derive iv via Random.new().read(AES.block_size), which is a per-encryption nondeterministic IV. No code sets a constant IV or calls Random.seed anywhere in the repository.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The protocol uses nonces/timestamps, but freshness is not enforced correctly: the server checks for replays but never records accepted nonces (so reuse cannot be prevented), the client's nonce-check only validates on success responses (error/return paths are not validated), and nonce-cache flushing code is buggy. These violate the test requirements (nonces not recorded / response value nonce not checked on error paths / nonce management bugs).
EVIDENCE: 
- Client generates and includes a nonce and timestamp in requests: [/workdir/repo/atm.py:108-113] (create_account) and similarly [/workdir/repo/atm.py:161-166] (deposit), [/workdir/repo/atm.py:204-209] (withdraw), [/workdir/repo/atm.py:247-251] (get_balance).
- Client only verifies the returned nonce on success paths (does not validate nonce on error/other return paths). Example: create_account checks nonce only when dec_list[0] == "1": [/workdir/repo/atm.py:124-139]. Same pattern occurs in deposit, withdraw, and get_balance: [/workdir/repo/atm.py:172-185], [/workdir/repo/atm.py:218-228], [/workdir/repo/atm.py:261-270]. This means error responses are not subject to nonce verification by the client.
- Server performs a replay/timestamp check using checkReplay (timestamp parsing and nonce membership check): [/workdir/repo/bank.py:123-133]. It also enforces a time window MAX_DELAY defined here: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:26].
- However, the server never records accepted nonces into its nonce table (bank.nonceData). The Bank class initializes the nonce store but there is no code that adds nonces upon accepting a request; see initialization: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:325-333]. Meanwhile, successful responses are sent back (including the nonce) at these lines — but without recording the nonce: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:262], [/workdir/repo/bank.py:274], [/workdir/repo/bank.py:283-284], [/workdir/repo/bank.py:302]. The absence of any assignment like bank.nonceData[nonce] = ... shows nonces are never stored.
- The nonce cleanup/flush code is buggy and would not work as intended even if nonces were stored: flushNonceData iterates incorrectly and uses literal string keys and incorrect timedelta usage: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:346-352]. The periodic cleaner that calls flushNonceData is present: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:358-363], but due to the bugs flush will not reliably remove/track entries.
- The server's checkReplay uses deltaTime.seconds which ignores days and does not correctly handle future timestamps or negative deltas, so the window check is fragile: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:123-128].
Conclusion: Because the server never records nonces (so replay prevention cannot work) and the client does not validate nonces on error/return paths, the repository fails the freshness requirements.

If you want, I can produce a small patch that records nonces on acceptance and tightens/checks the timestamp logic, plus add client checks for nonce on all response paths.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The server's encrypted responses have predictable, differing lengths depending on whether the response includes a balance (and on the number of digits in that balance). An attacker observing message lengths (or base64-encoded lengths) can distinguish success vs failure and can infer balance magnitude. This violates the property that observable metadata should not reveal an account's name or balance.

EVIDENCE:
- The AES encryption implementation base64-encodes iv + ciphertext, so ciphertext length depends on plaintext length (padding to AES block size) and thus on whether a balance field is present: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:159-166].
- The server writes responses with and without a balance in plaintext before encryption. Balance responses include ";balance:<amount>", while other successful responses do not: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:278-284] (balance response) and [/workdir/repo/bank.py:260-274, 300-303] (other success responses use "1;nonce:..." without balance). Error responses use different codes (e.g. "255;nonce:...") and are also encrypted and sent: [/workdir/repo/bank.py:309-316]. These differing plaintexts produce differing ciphertext lengths.
- Practical encryption output demonstrating the length differences was generated using the same encryption scheme and a fixed 16-byte key. The script used to reproduce the ciphertext lengths is saved at: /evidence/artifacts/encrypt_lengths.py and its output is saved at: /evidence/artifacts/encrypt_output.txt. The output shows base64 lengths 64 bytes for messages without balance ("failure" and "success_no_balance") and 88 bytes for messages that include balance values ("balance_10", "balance_1000", "balance_1000000"). See /evidence/artifacts/encrypt_output.txt for the concrete results.

Because ciphertext length (and thus observable message length) differs predictably between responses that include a balance and those that do not — and the length scales with the number of digits in the balance — an on-path observer can infer whether a balance was returned and approximate its magnitude. Therefore the test FAILs.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The server requires possession of the shared AES key (bank.auth) to produce properly encrypted transactions and it verifies message integrity and required credentials before executing privileged operations. For deposit/balance/withdraw the server explicitly checks the account/card PIN and card name (checkCard) before performing any state-modifying or privileged response, and ApplicationException/Exception handlers send error responses and do not perform the privileged effects.
EVIDENCE: 
- Server decrypts incoming transaction with the server key and parses fields before any action is taken: [/repo/bank.py:227-235] (aesCypher.decrypt, extractFields, account/action parsing) and [/repo/bank.py:236-240] (reading pin/nonce/cardname, checkReplay, checkHash).
- The server enforces credential checks before performing actions:
  - deposit: checkCard is called before updating the account balance and writing success response [/repo/bank.py:263-274] (checkCard then bank.accountList[...] update and response).
  - balance: checkCard is called before returning balance [/repo/bank.py:278-284].
  - withdraw: checkCard is called before deducting funds [/repo/bank.py:287-303].
- On credential/check failures the code takes the error path and writes error responses without applying privileged effects: ApplicationException handler writes an encrypted 255 error and releases locks [/repo/bank.py:309-313]; generic Exception handler writes 63 and exits [/repo/bank.py:313-318].
- The ATM client reads the same auth file and card file and constructs an AES-encrypted transaction including pin and nonce/hash before sending, demonstrating the intended authenticated channel and credential flow: [/repo/atm.py:98-107] (reading auth file and preparing URL), [/repo/atm.py:160-166] (encrypting payload), and examples of actions where card_file/pin are read and included in messages (e.g. [/repo/atm.py:151-158], [/repo/atm.py:246-252]).

Notes/limitations: Replay/tampering are out-of-scope per the test. The initial_balance operation creates new credentials (pin/cardname) but still requires the shared AES key to be present (bank.auth) to send an accepted request, so an unauthenticated client (no bank.auth) cannot trigger account creation either.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The bank HTTP handler can raise an uncaught exception during processing of malformed/attacker-controlled input: when AES decryption (or other early processing) fails, the handler's generic except block references the local variable `nonce` (and attempts to use `aesCypher`) before those variables are guaranteed to be assigned, causing an UnboundLocalError that crashes the request handling and disrupts protocol integrity.
EVIDENCE: 
- Runtime trace showing the uncaught exception (server output): [/evidence/artifacts/bank_stdout.txt:1-17]. The traceback demonstrates UnboundLocalError: local variable 'nonce' referenced before assignment, triggered while handling a POST with malformed transaction data.
- The handler code that constructs the error response and references `nonce`: [/repo/bank.py:313-318]. This is the except Exception block that attempts to write an encrypted error message using `nonce`.
- The decryption and assignment of `nonce` happen later in the normal flow (so a failure before that leaves `nonce` undefined): [/repo/bank.py:227-239]. If aesCypher.decrypt(cypheredData) raises, `nonce` is never set.
- A parsing helper that can raise on malformed fields without size checks (static issue): [/repo/bank.py:111-120] (extractFields uses field.split(":") and indexes nameValue[1] without checking length).

How I reproduced it (commands run):
1) Installed Python 2.7 and dependencies in the environment and started the server:
   python2 repo/bank.py -p 3001 > /evidence/artifacts/bank_stdout.txt 2>&1 & echo $! > /evidence/artifacts/bank_pid.txt
2) Sent a POST with an attacker-controlled malformed transaction (invalid base64):
   curl -v -X POST -d "transaction=!!!notbase64!!!" http://127.0.0.1:3001/

The server printed "protocol_error" and then the UnboundLocalError shown in [/evidence/artifacts/bank_stdout.txt:1-17]. This demonstrates an attacker-influenced runtime interaction leading to an uncaught exception and disruption of protocol handling.

Files created during testing: /evidence/artifacts/bank_stdout.txt (server output) and /evidence/artifacts/bank_pid.txt (server pid).

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository generates and stores per-card secrets as freshly-generated random 16-character alphanumeric strings (not as a hash of the account or any other public identifier). The card secret is written to a card file and later read from the card file to authenticate operations. This matches the test requirement that card values are not deterministically derived from public identifiers and contain randomness.

EVIDENCE:
- Card secret generation in ATM client: atm.py shows a generate_pin method that builds a length-N string by choosing characters from ascii_letters+digits and is used to create the card PIN [repo/atm.py:93-95, 108-114]. Specifically, atm.py creates pin = self.generate_pin(16) and includes it in the initial account creation request [repo/atm.py:108-114].
  - [repo/atm.py:93-95] generate_pin implementation
  - [repo/atm.py:108-114] pin generation and inclusion in data sent to server

- Card file creation: atm.py writes the generated pin to the card file returned from the server after account creation [repo/atm.py:128-135].
  - [repo/atm.py:128-135] open(card_file, "w") and f_card.write(pin)

- Card secret is used for authentication on operations: atm.py reads the card file and uses the stored pin for deposit/withdraw/get_balance requests [repo/atm.py:151-158, 238-245].
  - [repo/atm.py:151-158] reading pin for deposit
  - [repo/atm.py:238-245] reading pin for get_balance

- Server-side generation and storage of secrets: bank.py defines the same generate_pin function and uses it when creating the auth file; the bank stores the provided pin from the client as the account's card secret (not derived from account name) [repo/bank.py:30-36, 34-43, 256-259].
  - [repo/bank.py:30-36] generate_pin function
  - [repo/bank.py:34-43] createAuthFile writes a random pin to the auth file
  - [repo/bank.py:256-259] bank.accountCardList[account] = pin and bank.accountCardNameList[account] = cardName (server stores the client-provided random pin)

- No code deterministically deriving card secret from account name: the code paths show the pin is either generated (generate_pin) or read from a file. There is no code that computes a card secret as a hash of the account name (no assignment like pin = hashlib.sha256(account) or similar used as the card secret).
  - Searches and relevant assignments above demonstrate the pin comes from generate_pin or from a file write/read sequence.

Notes / confidence: Static inspection of the repository code provides direct evidence that card secrets are randomly generated 16-character alphanumeric strings and are not deterministic hashes of public identifiers. I did not run the code, since the static source is sufficient to verify the generation and storage logic. If you want an empirical check (for example to confirm the runtime RNG is cryptographically secure on the deployed environment), you can run the create-account flow and inspect a created card file; evidence to collect would be (a) a created card file under a test account showing a 16-char alphanumeric secret, and (b) server storage content showing the same secret associated with that account.

CITED FILES (with line ranges):
- /workdir/repo/repo/atm.py:93-95,108-114,128-135,151-158,238-245
- /workdir/repo/repo/bank.py:30-36,34-43,256-259,68-75

REASON: All runtime ATM<->Bank network transmissions are sent via the shared sendMessage/receiveMessage routines in common.py. sendMessage (common.py) encrypts the entire padded plaintext with AES-CBC (iv + ciphertext) and then appends an RSA signature; only the ciphertext+signature bytes are sent on the socket. receiveMessage requires the signature to verify the ciphertext and then decrypts it before parsing. The ATM and Bank both use these routines for all network I/O, and there are no other direct socket send/recv calls that transmit plaintext sensitive fields.

EVIDENCE:
- Sender: sendMessage constructs the plaintext, pads it, encrypts it with AES-CBC and sends ciphertext+signature: [/repo/common.py:31-49] (encrypt, signMessage, conn.send(signMessage(encrypt(tx))))
- Receiver: receiveMessage splits the received bytes into message and signature, verifies the signature, decrypts the message and only then parses it: [/repo/common.py:50-71] (messageReceived = conn.recv(609); checkSignature; decrypt; return msgParse(...))
- Message parsing and recognized sensitive fields (account, pin, $, action, timestamp) are defined and parsed only after decryption: [/repo/common.py:81-99] (msgParse and validTitles include 'account', '$', 'pin', 'action')

- Bank receives via receiveMessage and replies using sendMessage (so replies containing sensitive fields like balance are sent encrypted): [/repo/bank.py:119-132] (listen: receiveMessage used) and [/repo/bank.py:145-149] (sendReply uses sendMessage to send reply containing $ and pin when appropriate)

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The protocol uses timestamps but has critical flaws: (1) the bank accepts unbounded/overly-large timestamp values and stores them (allowing an attacker to set a timestamp to infinity), causing future legitimate requests to be rejected (a "Nonce overflows"/unbounded-nonce issue); (2) the ATM does not enforce freshness on error replies — validateBankAnswer returns an error when bankAns == 'n' before checking the timestamp, so freshness is not enforced on error/return paths (an "Ignore check failure" on error paths). Both findings are evidenced by code and a small runtime simulation.

EVIDENCE:
- Timestamp present in messages sent by ATM: [repo/atm.py:171-176] (ATM includes 'timestamp=' + self.timestamp when sending requests).
- Bank echoes/returns timestamp in replies: new-account and other replies include 'timestamp=' + self.fieldsDict['timestamp'] [repo/bank.py:151-166] and [repo/bank.py:169-181].
- Bank checks incoming timestamps and updates stored timestamp without bounds: the comparison and update are in validateIncomingOperation where the bank does "elif self.accountHolders[self.fieldsDict['account']]['timestamp'] >= float(self.fieldsDict['timestamp']): ... else: self.accountHolders[self.fieldsDict['account']]['timestamp'] = float(self.fieldsDict['timestamp'])" [repo/bank.py:236-246]. This shows the bank accepts any float-parsable timestamp and writes it into state.
- ATM checks reply freshness but ignores timestamp checks on error replies: validateBankAnswer first tests reply['bankAns'] == 'n' and raises before checking timestamp equality, so timestamps are not enforced on error return paths [repo/common.py:149-156]. The ATM calls validateBankAnswer after receiving replies [repo/atm.py:224-231]. This demonstrates that an error reply path does not validate freshness.
- Runtime simulation showing float overflow becomes inf and leads to stored timestamp = inf, causing later legitimate timestamps to be rejected (demonstrating the overflow/large-value acceptance issue). Reproduction output saved here: /evidence/artifacts/overflow_demo.txt (contents show attack_ts: inf and stored_ts >= legit_ts ? True after update).

Why this fails the test-case criteria:
- The protocol does use a freshness value (timestamp), but receivers do not robustly enforce bounds or check freshness on all acceptance/error paths. Accepting an unbounded timestamp permits an attacker to set a stored timestamp to infinity (or an excessively large value), preventing subsequent legitimate messages from being accepted. Additionally, ATM does not validate freshness on error responses, violating the requirement that freshness be enforced on all receipt paths.

Reproducible checks you can run locally:
- Inspect the code citations above to confirm the logic paths.
- See runtime reproduction at /evidence/artifacts/overflow_demo.txt which demonstrates float('1e400') -> inf and the subsequent rejection of legitimate timestamps.

Files referenced (verifyable):
- /workdir/repo/atm.py (calls validateBankAnswer): [repo/atm.py:224-231]
- /workdir/repo/bank.py (timestamp comparison & update): [repo/bank.py:236-246]; (reply timestamp inclusion) [repo/bank.py:151-166], [repo/bank.py:169-181]
- /workdir/repo/common.py (validateBankAnswer ordering): [repo/common.py:149-156]
- /evidence/artifacts/overflow_demo.txt (runtime simulation demonstrating float overflow -> inf and its effect)

Based on the concrete code paths and the runtime demonstration of float overflow behavior, the repository FAILs the freshness requirements in the test description.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: All ATM<->Bank runtime messages that influence control flow or state are protected by a keyed cryptographic signature (RSA PKCS#1 v1.5) and signature verification is enforced on every acceptance path, including error/return responses. Both directions (ATM->Bank and Bank->ATM) sign messages before sending and verify on receipt; invalid signatures raise ret63 and are handled (ATM exits with code 63; Bank prints protocol_error and does not process the message). Bank error responses are also produced via the same sendMessage path and therefore are signed.
EVIDENCE: 
- Signature creation (signing) is done in common.sendMessage: [repo/common.py:42-48] shows SHA hashing and PKCS1_v1_5 signer usage and sending the message+signature.
- Signature verification is done in common.receiveMessage: [repo/common.py:53-60] shows verifier.verify(...) and raising ret63 on failure; receiveMessage only returns the parsed message when checkSignature succeeds [repo/common.py:67-70].
- ATM sends signed messages and expects signed replies: sendMessage called with ATM private key and AES key in ATM.sendMessageToBank: [repo/atm.py:224-228]. The ATM calls receiveMessage (which verifies signature) and then validateBankAnswer on the verified reply [repo/atm.py:226-228]. ATM handles verification failures by exiting on ret63: [repo/atm.py:233-240].
- Bank verifies incoming ATM messages before processing: Bank.listen2network calls receiveMessage(...) and only then treatMessage(...); verification failures raise ret63 which the Bank catches and prints 'protocol_error' and does not call treatMessage: [repo/bank.py:119-137].
- Bank sends signed replies (including on error paths): Bank.sendReply uses sendMessage with the bank private key to send both success and failure replies [repo/bank.py:145-149]. Bank.error branches call sendReply(False) (examples: validateIncomingOperation and treatNewAccount) so error responses are signed as well [repo/bank.py:223-233] and [repo/bank.py:151-156].
- The cryptographic primitives used (imports) indicate keyed signature usage: [repo/common.py:11-15] (AES, PKCS1_v1_5, SHA, RSA).

These artifacts show keyed authentication is present and enforced before any state-changing logic or acceptance, and that replies (including error replies) are produced via the same signed sending function. Therefore the test passes.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The repository pads every plaintext reply to a fixed length before encryption and then appends a fixed-size RSA signature, producing a constant-length wire message for both successful and failed responses. I ran a small runtime test (using the repo's common.sendMessage implementation, with minor Py3 compatibility patches only for local testing) which showed that success and failure replies produced identical total message lengths (608 bytes). Because the total on-wire length is constant, a MitM cannot distinguish success vs failure or infer account balances from message length differences.

EVIDENCE:
1) Padding and fixed plaintext length in the code: [/repo/common.py:29-35] shows LENGTH_OF_ALL_PLAINTEXTS = 336 and that sendMessage pads the plaintext to that length.
2) Encryption + IV + signature leading to constant total length: [/repo/common.py:36-51] shows the encrypt and signMessage functions and the conn.send(signMessage(encrypt(tx))) call (encrypt uses a 16-byte IV; AES block-size padding makes ciphertext length equal to LENGTH_OF_ALL_PLAINTEXTS). The receive side reads a fixed buffer size: [/repo/common.py:53-55] (messageReceived = conn.recv(609)) and expects the encrypted part at [0:352] and signature at [352:], see [/repo/common.py:70-75]. Together these imply encrypted payload = 16 (IV) + 336 (plaintext) = 352 bytes, plus a 2048-bit RSA signature = 256 bytes, total 608 bytes on the wire.
3) All replies use the same sendMessage path: [/repo/bank.py:145-149] (sendReply constructs replyText then calls sendMessage) and the ATM uses the same framing when sending/receiving: [/repo/atm.py:224-228]. Thus both success and failure responses are produced via the same fixed-length sendMessage path.
4) Runtime test artifact showing identical lengths for example success and failure messages: /evidence/artifacts/msg_length_test.txt (contains the printed lengths from the test: len(success_msg) = 608, len(fail_msg) = 608, and the breakdown of components).

Notes / caveats:
- I made minimal, local-only compatibility edits to common.py so I could run the runtime check under Python3 (ensuring plaintext/keys are bytes). Those edits were strictly to allow local testing and do not change the protocol semantics (padding, IV, and signature behavior remain the same). The static code evidence alone already demonstrates the fixed-length behavior for on-wire messages in the repository.
- This test only checks whether message length metadata leaks account name/balance info via differing lengths. It does not evaluate other metadata channels (timing, connection counts, etc.). The test statement excluded encryption absence as out-of-scope; here the protocol already encrypts and signs messages and pads them to a fixed plaintext length before encryption, which prevents length-based leaks as described.

Artifacts:
- /evidence/artifacts/msg_length_test.txt (runtime outputs confirming equal lengths)
- Code citations above showing the padding, encryption, signature, and fixed recv buffer.

Conclusion: PASS — the implementation pads and signs replies so that on-wire message lengths are constant between success and failure, preventing a MitM from distinguishing account/balance via message-length metadata.

VERDICT: PASS
REASON: The bank server enforces channel authentication (message signature + AES decryption) and verifies request credentials (account PIN and timestamp) before performing privileged actions. Unauthenticated or improperly authenticated requests are rejected (protocol error) and requests with missing/incorrect credentials do not cause withdrawals/deposits/balance changes.
EVIDENCE: 
- Authentication enforced at receive + signature/crypto: [repo/common.py:50-71] implements receiveMessage that checks signature and decrypts; signature failures raise ret63 which prevents further processing.
- Server rejects protocol/auth failures and does not execute actions: [repo/bank.py:119-143] shows listen2network calling receiveMessage inside try/except and printing "protocol_error" on ret63, and closing the connection without invoking action handlers.
- Credentials checked before privileged effects: [repo/bank.py:223-246] validateIncomingOperation returns False (and sends negative reply) if account missing, if PIN mismatch, or if timestamp invalid; action handlers (deposit/withdraw/getBalance) call validateIncomingOperation before performing updates [repo/bank.py:169, 184, 202].
- Runtime traces showing behavior:
  - Bank created auth and accepted legitimate account creation: [/evidence/artifacts/atm_create_log.txt] contains '{"account":"alice","initial_balance":100.00}' showing account created by an authenticated ATM.
  - An unauthenticated raw TCP message produced "protocol_error" and did not change balance: [/evidence/artifacts/bank_log.txt] contains 'protocol_error' and subsequent legitimate balance check shows balance still 100.00 in [/evidence/artifacts/atm_balance_log.txt] and [/evidence/artifacts/atm_balance2.txt].
  - A signed message missing the PIN (sent using the ATM private key but with missing credential) did not trigger withdrawal; the helper client output is in [/evidence/artifacts/missing_pin_out.txt] (script printed 'sent') and the balance remained 100.00 as shown in the ATM balance logs above.

Concrete artifacts saved under /evidence/artifacts/ (bank_log.txt, atm_create_log.txt, atm_balance_log.txt, atm_balance2.txt, missing_pin_out.txt) allow independent verification. Code citations show where authentication and credential checks are enforced, and the runtime logs demonstrate that unauthenticated or missing/failed credentials do not cause privileged effects.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The code performs size-dependent slicing and dereferences message structures without adequate validation of received buffer lengths or the return values of receiveMessage. This allows attacker-controlled inputs (short or malformed messages, or abrupt connection close/timeouts) to trigger exceptions that propagate to high-level control flow and can disrupt protocol integrity (e.g. client/server lacking a reply, client exiting with error). These are reachable from normal network interactions.
EVIDENCE: 
- Missing packet-size validation before slicing the received buffer: common.receiveMessage reads a fixed-size buffer and slices it into signature/message parts without ensuring the buffer is long enough. See [/repo/common.py:50-71]:
  - Line 50: messageReceived = conn.recv(609)
  - Line 67: if len(messageReceived):
  - Line 69: return msgParse(decrypt(checkSignature(messageReceived[0:352], messageReceived[352:])))
  This code slices messageReceived[0:352] and messageReceived[352:] even when len(messageReceived) < 352 — no explicit length check for >=352, only truthiness of the buffer. An attacker-controlled short packet can thus trigger signature/decrypt/parse errors.

- receiveMessage does not catch socket.recv exceptions (e.g. socket.timeout). The conn.recv call is not wrapped in try/except, so socket.timeout or other socket errors will propagate to the caller. See [/repo/common.py:50-52].

- Caller uses receiveMessage return value without validation: atm.sendMessageToBank takes reply = receiveMessage(...) and immediately calls validateBankAnswer(reply, ...), which assumes reply is a dict and indexes into it. If receiveMessage returns None (for empty recv) or if a socket.timeout propagated, validateBankAnswer will raise (TypeError or other). See [/repo/atm.py:224-228] and [/repo/common.py:149-157]:
  - [/repo/atm.py:224-228]:
    224	def sendMessageToBank(self, message):
    225		self.s.connect((self.ipAddress, self.port))
    226		sendMessage(self.s, message, sEncryptionKey=self.AESKey, sSignatureKey=self.secretKey)
    227		reply = receiveMessage(self.s, sEncryptionKey=self.AESKey, sSignatureKey=self.bankPublicKey)
    228		validateBankAnswer(reply, self.atmID, self.timestamp)

  - [/repo/common.py:149-157]:
    149	def validateBankAnswer(reply, atmID, timestamp):
    150		if reply['bankAns'] == 'n':
    151			debug('Error in operation')
    152			raise ret255
    153		elif reply['timestamp'] != timestamp:
    154			debug('Error in timestamp validation')
    155			raise ret255
    156		elif reply['atmID'] != atmID:
    157			debug('Error in atm validation')
    158			raise ret255

  If reply is None or otherwise malformed, indexing reply['bankAns'] will raise an uncaught exception in the immediate scope of sendMessageToBank.

- Top-level exception handling: the ATM script does include a top-level catch-all (except:) which causes the process to exit with -1 (see [/repo/atm.py:233-244]). However, that still results in process termination and broken client-side protocol state; abrupt termination of the client constitutes a disruption of protocol integrity. The presence of the top-level except does not prevent the underlying issue (receiving malformed/short packets or connection timeouts can still terminate the client process). See [/repo/atm.py:233-244].

Dynamic execution attempt and environment note:
- I attempted to run dynamic repros, but the repository is Python 2 code and the environment lacks a python2 interpreter. I installed pycryptodome to inspect and (attempt to) generate keys, but could not run the scripts under python2 here. That said, the static code-level evidence above is sufficient to demonstrate the defect.

Conclusion: The repository FAILs the test because attacker-controlled network input can cause unvalidated slicing and dereferencing, leading to exceptions that disrupt protocol integrity (client termination or missing replies).
